title: Trinity: One Differentiable Physics for Training, Refining and Scoring Generative Floorplanners

paper.title: Trinity: One Differentiable Physics for Training, Refining and Scoring Generative Floorplanners
paper.abstract: Abstract Floorplanning arranges the blocks of a chip and decides their shapes under objectives that press blocks together, short wirelength and a small outline, and constraints that hold them apart, non-overlap, clusters, MIB shapes and boundary blocks. Recent diffusion placers train on reference layouts alone and leave this coupled system to guidance, post-hoc loops and a legalizer, reporting only the endpoint, which hides what the generator contributes. We re-implement four of them under one recipe on FloorSet, score raw, refined and legalized layouts on one scale, and propose Trinity, a flow-matching floorplanner whose six differentiable functions for the constraints and objectives are its training loss term, the energy of a closed-form refiner after sampling and the base of a soft cost for every stage. The network thus learns the correction prior placers apply in their samplers, and sampling needs no guidance. Stage by stage, the training term lowers a plain transformer’s raw soft cost by 26% and matters most at short budgets, the shared refiner decides more of the final cost than the generator and matches a ported placer’s loop in 16 to 660 times fewer steps, Trinity’s refined soft cost is 36% below the best ported pipeline, the soft cost ranks settings as the contest’s hard cost does, and on the FloorSet val set the pipeline reaches a mean hard cost of 1.014 in 1.63 s per case.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Floorplanning is an early stage of the physical design flow in Electronic Design Automation (EDA). Given a netlist and each block’s target area, floorplanning arranges the position and shape of every block on the chip, and the floorplan bounds what each later stage can achieve. A floorplanner pursues two objectives, short wirelength between connected blocks and a small outline area , and must reach them under hard constraints: a floorplan is feasible only if every block matches its target area, fixed-shape blocks retain their shapes, pre-placed blocks remain in place, and no two blocks overlap. Three soft constraints follow in practice: blocks of a cluster should stay adjacent, multi-instance blocks (MIB) should share one shape, and boundary blocks should touch the die boundary ( ICCAD, 2026 ) . The objectives and constraints pull in opposite directions, and the strongest floorplans sit where the hard constraints bind. Learning-based methods promise to amortize this per-instance optimization into a trained model. Floorplanning moreover suits a generative treatment: an instance admits many strong layouts rather than one optimum, and a generative model drafts complete layouts from this distribution ( Lee et al., 2025 ; Trung and Hy, 2026 ; Yoon et al., 2026 ; Xie et al., 2026 ) . However, such a model learns the distribution of reference layouts rather than the geometry of a single one: a network trained with a squared loss estimates a conditional mean of the reference layouts given its input, and a mean of feasible layouts is not necessarily feasible, since the feasible set is nonconvex. An infeasible draft leaves the constraints to corrections applied after sampling. Such corrections act on a landscape whose couplings belong to floorplanning itself rather than any model: as blocks compete for the same die area, a step that resolves an overlap can scatter a cluster or displace a pre-placed block, and a push toward feasibility may sacrifice the wirelength and outline area that the objectives demand. A generative floorplanner must therefore treat the constraints and objectives as one coupled system, and where this system enters the pipeline determines what the model learns. Existing methods differ in where they place this coupled system, and each choice carries its own cost. Classic floorplanners place it inside the search procedure: simulated annealing ( Wong and Liu, 1986 ) explores topological representations such as the sequence pair ( Murata et al., 1996 ) and the B ∗ -tree ( Chang et al., 2000 ) , in which non-overlap holds by construction, and analytical placement ( Lu et al., 2015 ; Lin et al., 2021 ) minimizes a differentiable relaxation of overlap jointly with wirelength. Since every move faces the constraints and the objectives together, these solvers remain on the boundary, at the price of a search that begins anew on every netlist. Learning-based methods lift this per-instance cost, and the constraints begin to recede from training. Reinforcement learning stays nearest to the classic position, with the constraints written into its actions and the objectives into its reward ( Mirhoseini et al., 2021 ; Lai et al., 2022 ; Lai et al., 2023 ) , although the two do not meet in one function that the policy learns, and the agent is retrained or fine-tuned for every new netlist. Regression abandons the constraints and trains on reference layouts alone ( Liu et al., 2023b ; Amini et al., 2022 ) , which leaves the model exposed to the conditional-mean difficulty above. The recent diffusion placers ( Lee et al., 2025 ; Trung and Hy, 2026 ; Yoon et al., 2026 ; Xie et al., 2026 ) push this coupled system farthest from training: their losses only reproduce the reference layouts, and every correction arrives after the model. The first of these corrections, a hand-tuned guidance term, intervenes during sampling. The finished sample then enters post-hoc optimization loops, and the remaining violations are left to the legalizer. Fig. 1 (left) draws this arrangement. These placers come from macro placement, a task where every shape is fixed: the shape freedom of floorplanning, and its soft constraints, stay outside their scope. The network’s contribution is not measured stage by stage: their papers examine only the endpoint of the pipeline, and each stage expresses the constraints in its own form, which leaves the intermediate layouts without a common measure. At that endpoint, a weak generator behind a strong correction and a strong generator behind a weak one appear identical. The constraints thus migrate from the core of the classic search to the tail of the correction chain. Among the generative placers, the constraints have appeared everywhere except the training loss. Their place in that loss, and its effect on every later stage, nevertheless remain unexplored. Given these observations, the remedy is to move the coupled system into training itself. The constraints can enter the training loss directly, since every objective and constraint of floorplanning measures a geometric quantity of the layout and admits a differentiable expression in the positions and shapes of the blocks. The overlap between two blocks, for instance, shrinks continuously as they separate and reaches zero exactly when the pair satisfies the non-overlap constraint. A weighted sum of these expressions defines an energy, one function that records the constraints and objectives together with the trade-off between them. The energy therefore assigns every layout a graded value rather than a binary indicator of feasibility. Analytical placement already minimizes an energy of this form that couples overlap with wirelength ( Kleinhans et al., 1991 ; Lu et al., 2015 ; Lin et al., 2021 ) . A generative floorplanner can instead place such an energy in its training loss, where each gradient step responds to the reference layouts and the coupled system together. After training, the same expressions determine what a later refinement minimizes and provide a common measure for the layout that each stage produces ( Fig. 1 , middle). On this measure, the intermediate layouts reveal how much the generator and each later stage contribute, a distinction that the endpoint alone conceals. To expose this distinction and place the coupled system in training rather than leave it to corrections after sampling, we propose Trinity , a flow-matching floorplanner whose six differentiable functions for the constraints and objectives are incorporated into its training loss, serve as the energy of its refiner, and form the basis of a soft cost that scores the layout of every stage. Trained with these functions, the network learns the correction that prior placers apply inside their samplers, and sampling runs without guidance ( Section 3 ). Measured stage by stage, the pipeline reveals distinct roles for training and refinement: the training term contributes most when the refinement budget is short, and the refiner accounts for more of the final cost than the generator does. Added to the training of a plain transformer, the six functions alone lower the soft cost of its raw samples by 26% ( Section 4.2 ). With our refiner shared across the generators of four diffusion placers ported to our training recipe, their final costs converge despite a wide spread in raw costs, and on a ported placer’s samples, the refiner reaches the soft cost of that placer’s own loop in 16 to 660 times fewer iterations ( Fig. 1 , right). A comparison of generators therefore calls for a shared refiner. Against the ported pipelines with their own post-hoc loops, the full pipeline of Trinity reaches a refined soft cost 36% below the best of them ( Section 4.3 ). After legalization, Trinity remains ahead of these pipelines under the hard cost of the official contest ( ICCAD, 2026 ) , and on its validation set it reaches a mean hard cost of 1.014 at 1.63 seconds per case on one GPU with parallel legalization ( Section 4.4 ). Contributions. (1) We locate the limit of generative placers in the position of their physics rather than the strength of their networks: the coupled objectives and constraints of floorplanning enter every stage except the training loss. Trinity instead trains on the coupled system directly, with one energy built from six differentiable functions of the layout, and feasibility becomes a property the network learns rather than one that corrections restore. (2) We establish the theory behind this choice: a network trained on reference layouts alone estimates a conditional mean that the nonconvex feasible set does not necessarily contain, whereas the energy term in training approximates constraint guidance inside the sampling loop at no sampling cost. The same analysis selects the clean prediction as the head, the one output an energy can score, and experiment confirms each prediction. (3) We replace the hand-tuned correction loops of prior placers with a refiner that descends the training energy itself, every gradient in closed form. One refiner serves every generator: it carries Trinity and each ported placer below the final cost their own loops reach, and supplies the common ground for comparing generators. (4) We extend the scale of the contest beyond feasibility: our soft cost keeps the objective factor of the hard cost and admits overlap and soft-constraint severity as smooth penalties, and every stage’s layout shares one scale. Since the soft cost agrees with the hard cost on which settings perform better, the sampling and refinement budget can be chosen before the legalizer runs. (5) We lift the fixed-shape assumption that diffusion placers inherited from macro placement: Trinity treats positions and shapes alike and covers the full constraint family of floorplanning, from soft and pre-placed blocks to clusters, boundary blocks, and shared multi-instance shapes, and on the contest’s validation set the full pipeline surpasses the classical annealer at a fraction of its runtime.

sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: Classical optimization and direct learned placement construct layouts through per-instance search, sequential decisions, or joint coordinate prediction: simulated annealing explores sequence pairs and B ∗ -trees ( Wong and Liu, 1986 ; Murata et al., 1996 ; Chang et al., 2000 ; Lin and Chang, 2001 ; Adya and Markov, 2003 ) , analytical placement couples a continuous relaxation of overlap with legalization ( Kleinhans et al., 1991 ; Chen et al., 2008a ; Lu et al., 2015 ; Lin et al., 2021 ) , sequential construction commits one macro per decision under reinforcement learning ( Mirhoseini et al., 2021 ; Cheng and Yan, 2021 ; Lai et al., 2022 ; Lai et al., 2023 ; Geng et al., 2024 ; Geng et al., 2025 ; Gao et al., 2026 ; Shi et al., 2023 ) , and joint prediction regresses every block position from the netlist graph ( Liu et al., 2023b ; Amini et al., 2022 ) . Across the learned lines, block shapes stay fixed at placement time, whereas FloorSet requires the placer to settle a shape for every soft block ( Mallappa et al., 2024 ) . Generative macro placement keeps the fixed-shape setting and learns layout distributions through noise or velocity prediction, with geometric corrections during or after sampling: velocity-based FlowPlace ( Xie et al., 2026 ) applies overlap-free grid projection at each step, while the noise-based MacroDiff+ ( Yoon et al., 2026 ) , ChipDiffusion ( Lee et al., 2025 ) , and DiffPlace ( Trung and Hy, 2026 ) steer sampling with overlap and wirelength gradient guidance before post-hoc loops and legalization. On the objective side, linear transformations between data and noise connect flow matching ( Lipman et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2023a ) , interpolants ( Ma et al., 2024 ) , and noise prediction ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Nichol and Dhariwal, 2021 ; Salimans and Ho, 2022 ) , LACE ( Chen et al., 2024 ) and physics-informed diffusion ( Bastek et al., 2025 ) supervise the clean prediction with constraint losses, and Diffusion Transformers ( Peebles and Xie, 2023 ) supply the backbone, conditioned on the netlist through Graphormer-style attention bias ( Ying et al., 2021 ) , GraphGPS-style message passing ( Rampášek et al., 2022 ) , and Laplacian positional encoding ( Dwivedi and Bresson, 2020 ; Kreuzer et al., 2021 ; Dwivedi et al., 2022 ) . Following JiT ( Li and He, 2026 ) , Trinity predicts the clean layout and trains on the velocity it implies. For variable-shape floorplanning, it combines netlist-conditioned clean prediction in a DiT backbone with constraint supervision through one set of geometric functions for training, refinement, and scoring, and it scores raw, refined, and legalized layouts separately. Section A.4 surveys these lines in full.

sections.heading: 3.3 Framework Overview
sections.text: The framework shares a single set of physics functions across all three components: the generator trains on them, the refiner descends them, and the soft cost derived from them scores every stage on one scale (Figure 2 ). Trinity expresses each constraint and objective once as a function ℰ k \mathcal{E}_{k} of the decoded boxes, positions and shapes alike and dimensionless in the layout scale s s : a constraint function is zero when its rule holds, the intersection area over every pair of blocks, the gap to contact along a spanning tree of each cluster, the deviation of each MIB member from the median aspect of its group, and the distance of every boundary-coded side to its edge, while the wirelength and the outline area carry the objectives (Appendix E.1 ). The weighted sum U = ∑ k ω k ​ ℰ k U=\sum_{k}\omega_{k}\,\mathcal{E}_{k} is the physics term of the generator’s loss, the energy the refiner descends and the base of the soft cost of Section 3.1 (Figure 1 , middle). It depends only on the constraint annotations and the netlist and never on the reference layout, and thus supervises the network with the rules rather than the reference answer. Pipeline (right): each draw passes the generator, the refiner and the legalizer, top to bottom in each column. Generator. The generator drafts complete layouts from noise, conditioned on the netlist, and carries the physics term in its training loss. A DiT ( Peebles and Xie, 2023 ) with one token per block and the time step as a token ( Bao et al., 2023 ) . The netlist enters as an additive attention bias ( Ying et al., 2021 ) , through the information mover, a gated one-hop graph convolution on the residual stream ( Kipf and Welling, 2017 ; Rampášek et al., 2022 ) , and as two Laplacian eigenvectors in the input coordinates ( Dwivedi and Bresson, 2020 ; Kreuzer et al., 2021 ) (Appendix B.3 ). Following JiT ( Li and He, 2026 ) , the network predicts the clean layout x ^ 0 \hat{x}_{0} and trains on its implied velocity, with t t logit-normal ( Esser et al., 2024 ) , m m the padding mask and the weights λ \lambda , ω k \omega_{k} of Section 4.1 , as follows: ℒ = 𝔼 t , x 0 , x 1 ​ [ ℒ fm + λ ​ U ​ ( x ^ 0 ) ] , ℒ fm = ‖ ( x t − x ^ 0 t − ( x 1 − x 0 ) ) ⊙ m ‖ 2 2 . \mathcal{L}=\mathbb{E}_{t,\,x_{0},\,x_{1}}\bigl[\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{fm}}+\lambda\,U(\hat{x}_{0})\bigr],\qquad\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{fm}}=\bigl\|\bigl(\tfrac{x_{t}-\hat{x}_{0}}{t}-(x_{1}-x_{0})\bigr)\odot m\bigr\|_{2}^{2}. (3) The clean head keeps the physics term inexpensive, since the loss needs a decoded layout and x ^ 0 \hat{x}_{0} is one, whereas a velocity head reaches the same minimizer through a gradient scaled by − t -t and a target that still contains the noise (Proposition D.3 ), which Section 4.2 measures. Sampling follows plain Euler in uniform steps from t = 1 t=1 to 0 0 over NFE \mathrm{NFE} evaluations with no guidance term, and after every step the known answers of the instance enter the sample, a fixed-shape block keeping its ρ i \rho_{i} , a pre-placed block all three coordinates and the blocks of a MIB group the mean of their predicted ρ i \rho_{i} . Refiner. The refiner descends the training energy explicitly once sampling ends, at negligible cost. From each sample at t = 0 t=0 , the refiner takes K K steps of Adam ( Kingma and Ba, 2015 ) on U U under a heavier overlap weight than training, every gradient evaluated in closed form and the same sampling overrides written back after every step. Refinement thus resumes the descent of U U where the proximal step of Proposition 3.1 has vanished at t = 0 t=0 (schedule, sweep and running cost in Appendix E ). Legalizer. The legalizer converts each refined layout into a hard-feasible one while penalizing the displacement it introduces. A sequence-pair relation, under which non-overlap holds by construction, is extracted for every pair of blocks from the refined layout, and one linear program positions the blocks at their decoded shapes under those relations, with the pre-placed blocks pinned, cluster members abutting along a spanning tree of the cluster and coded sides on the outline, and minimizes the chip outline plus the displacement from the refined positions ( Murata et al., 1996 ; Murata and Kuh, 1998 ) . An infeasible program first relaxes the soft rules, flips the conflicting relations and re-solves the program within a bounded number of rounds, and a final contact snap that moves a block only where no overlap appears completes each draw at a hard-feasible final layout (Appendix F ).

sections.heading: 4 Experimental Results
sections.text: The experiments evaluate every stage, since endpoint quality alone cannot identify the generator’s contribution. Raw, refined, and legalized layouts therefore share the one scale of Section 3.1 , which tests whether pre-legalization quality persists in feasible layouts and separates generator quality from later optimization. Appendices H to M hold the full tables, Appendix N every data view.

sections.heading: 4.1 Experimental Setup
sections.text: Benchmarks/Datasets. We train on MIB-consistent FloorSet-Lite ( Mallappa et al., 2024 ) , whose 996,000 synthetic floorplans span 21 to 120 blocks per instance. Unless stated otherwise, every reported number on our held-out validation set of 12,000 cases averages four draws per case and then across all cases. We evaluate separately on the official FloorSet val set of 100 cases for the official comparison in Table 8 and run one full GSRC evaluation as an external check in Table 8 . Baselines. We re-implement ChipDiffusion ( Lee et al., 2025 ) , DiffPlace ( Trung and Hy, 2026 ) , MacroDiff+ ( Yoon et al., 2026 ) , and FlowPlace ( Xie et al., 2026 ) as comparisons within the learned generative line. Under one training recipe, the ported placers retain their networks, objectives, and post-hoc loops while adopting our latent representation, conditioning, Euler sampler, and overrides, as specified in Section B.4 . The generator comparison excludes sampler-time guidance, which Appendix J evaluates on its own, and grid projection, whereas Section 4.3 includes the post-hoc loops under their released settings. To examine conditional-mean prediction, Reg- z z and Reg- x ​ y ​ w ​ h xywh predict latents and raw boxes on our backbone, with details in Appendix K.2 . The classical comparison uses the FloorSet team’s PARSAC annealer ( Mostafa et al., 2024 ) only on the FloorSet val set, since its published budget of 10 7 10^{7} steps per worker is prohibitive at the 12,000-case scale, with details in Appendix L . Metrics. We evaluate every layout by the quantities in Section 3.1 for cross-stage comparison, with soft cost derived from the shared differentiable physics and hard cost restricted to feasible layouts after legalization. We also report FLD and MMD for the generator comparison as reference-distribution distances, with scoring details in Appendix C . We report first-draw hard costs apart from best-of- N N hard costs selected by hard cost among the N N draws, with full tables in Appendices G to O . Implementation Details. Our three recurring comparisons distinguish the plain control, a plain transformer with a clean-sample head and no physics, from full Trinity with two graph components, six functions, and λ = 0.01 \lambda{=}0.01 , and from Trinity at λ = 0 \lambda{=}0 , the Trinity configuration without physics. All 66 models share a training recipe of 200,000 steps with batch size 256 and AdamW at an initial learning rate of 2 × 10 − 4 2\times 10^{-4} with cosine decay. This shared recipe uses exponential moving average (EMA) weights and augmentation by rotation, flip, shift, constraint dropout, and wire dropout at ten GPU-hours per model on one RTX 5090, the machine behind every reported timing. The legalizer runs on 16 CPU workers in parallel, and every training ω k \omega_{k} equals one, with further training details in Appendix B.2 . We sample with NFE ∈ { 1 , 2 , 4 , 8 , 16 , 32 } \mathrm{NFE}\in\{1,2,4,8,16,32\} and cap refinement at 400 Adam steps under a tenfold overlap weight, which keeps the sampling and refinement budgets distinct. sections.heading: 4.2 Raw Generator Quality before Refinement
sections.text: Table 1 compares the generator’s design choices, while Fig. 3 reports the contribution of physics training to raw-sample quality. The clean-sample head exposes a layout for direct energy evaluation, which ties its practical role to the theoretical choice of head. The information mover complements this choice through improved constraint objectives. Joint physics training improves every constraint metric without sacrificing the backbone’s wirelength or area. The resulting configuration combines the only head with a valid single-step layout and all six physics functions for the best trade-off. These gains persist down to the parameter count of the ported networks, where depth contributes more than width ( Figs. 3 , 5 and O ). The improvement also exceeds the variation across seeds in Appendices M and H . This stability thus supports the contribution of the shared differentiable physics at the raw stage, where its role in training is assessed ahead of any refinement. After a few hundred refinement steps, samples from every sampling budget reach nearly the same soft cost, which supports a low-budget draw followed by refinement, while the training physics keeps a substantial short-budget advantage over the λ = 0 \lambda{=}0 backbone ( Appendix I ), the training contribution that an endpoint comparison alone would conceal. Fig. 6 traces constraint improvement under the shared refiner against the ported placers’ released-loop outcomes, with wirelength and area preserved in Table 3 . In Fig. 4 , ChipDiffusion’s loop trades overlap for a wider cluster gap, whereas our refiner removes overlap without opening the cluster, which supports one set of six physics quantities across training, refinement and scoring. On the references, Fig. 5 (b)–(c) separates corrective refinement from motion that degrades the objectives: our refiner moves movable blocks by 0.0055 of the scale and lowers soft cost in 85% of cases, whereas the released loops move them by 0.025 to 0.029 and raise the cost in every case from 1.065 to 1.54 to 2.58 through wirelength and area, in line with the small-step account of Proposition 3.2 (ii) ( Appendix G ). On a ported generator’s samples our refiner matches the own-loop soft cost in a fraction of the steps and the time, and 400 of its steps carry each generator below its own loop’s endpoint, with or without its guidance ( Tables 3 and 5 , Appendix J ). Table 10 compares the cost of matching each ported placer’s own-loop soft cost with iteration counts and per-step time, not wall-clock measurements. The training term thus governs raw layouts and short-budget quality, and the refiner the converged endpoint.

sections.heading: 4.4 Legalized Layouts and the Official Hard Cost
sections.text: Table 3 and Table 8 compare legalized outcomes for the ported pipelines and for generators under a shared refiner, respectively. The advantage of Trinity over the ported placers persists in the official hard cost on feasible layouts, while the compression of generator differences under the shared refiner shows why endpoint comparisons understate generator quality. The narrowed differences indicate that refinement determines much of the final hard cost, ( Appendix K ). This dependence on refinement motivates comparing generators under a shared refiner within the stage-by-stage evaluation. Fig. 7 (b)–(d) traces the relation between soft cost and legalized hard cost that supports this stage-by-stage evaluation. Agreement between the two costs supports the soft cost as a proxy for comparing settings, with caution for individual draws early in refinement. Across the evaluated Trinity settings, mean soft and hard costs correlate strongly across the generator lines ( Table 10 ). At the individual-draw level, the initially weaker correlation improves as refinement produces samples that are easier to legalize. The soft cost therefore evaluates generators and refiners without a legalizer run for every experiment. Table 8 and Table 8 report the practical performance and transfer limits of the resulting legalized layouts. On FloorSet, the hard cost of Trinity approaches the reference cost at a small fraction of the computation PARSAC spends, consistent with Fig. 7 (a). Within the GSRC training range, the variant without the physics term matches the full model, as expected in distribution. Beyond that range, the six terms separate the variants and carry the model to larger block counts. At still larger sizes, no current checkpoint fits the outline ( Section G.4 ). The remaining limit therefore lies in the training range rather than the physics itself, which supports transfer beyond that range in the evaluated cases.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: Generative floorplanners placed the coupled objectives and constraints of floorplanning everywhere except where the model learns, and endpoint scores hid what each stage contributed. Trinity moved the coupled system into training: one energy of six differentiable functions served as a term of its loss, as the energy its refiner descends in closed form, and as the base of a soft cost that scored every stage, so sampling ran without guidance. Measured on that one scale, training and refinement played distinct roles. The training term improved every raw constraint at once and mattered most at short refinement budgets, while the refiner decided most of the final cost and carried every ported generator below its own loop in far fewer steps. Generators were therefore best compared under a shared refiner, and the soft cost, which ranked settings as the hard cost does, supported that comparison before legalization. With positions and shapes treated alike, Trinity covers the full constraint family of floorplanning and stays ahead of the ported pipelines after legalization.

sections.heading: AI use statement
sections.text: Generative AI tools were used for writing assistance, drafting passages and correcting grammar, and for visualizing results, where they wrote the plotting code that renders the figures from the result files. The authors reviewed every AI-assisted passage and figure and take responsibility for the content.

sections.heading: Reproducibility statement
sections.text: Every trained model in this paper, the ported prior placers included, uses the frozen recipe of Section 4.1 and Appendix B.2 . The six constraint quantities, the refiner and the legalizer are specified in Section 3 and Appendices E and F , and every scoring rule in Appendix C . FloorSet and the ICCAD 2026 evaluator are public. The supplementary material is the code needed to reproduce the study, the solver-agnostic domain library and the generator library, with the configuration file of every trained arm, every refiner sweep and every legalizer run, and the scripts that print every table from what a run writes (Appendix R ).

sections.heading: A.1 The Physical Design Flow
sections.text: A chip goes from a netlist, the gates and macros of the design and the nets that connect them, to a geometric layout through a fixed sequence of stages: partitioning, floorplanning, placement, clock tree synthesis, routing and timing closure ( Kahng et al., 2011 ) . Floorplanning is the first geometric stage. The design is partitioned into a few tens to a few hundred blocks, hard macros such as memories and IP whose shape is fixed and soft blocks of synthesized logic whose area is an estimate and whose aspect ratio is free within limits ( Otten, 1982 ; Stockmeyer, 1983 ) , and floorplanning decides the position of every block and the shape of every soft one. Placement then arranges the standard cells inside the blocks into rows of sites, tens of thousands to millions of cells of one height and fixed shape ( Markov et al., 2015 ) , and routing realizes every net as wires on the metal layers under capacity and spacing rules ( Kahng et al., 2011 ) . Figure 8 (top) sketches the three. They differ in what they move and in what binds them: floorplanning moves tens to a few hundred blocks and the shapes of the soft ones under non-overlap, fixed shapes, pre-placed blocks and the design constraints of Section 1 , placement moves 10 5 10^{5} to 10 7 10^{7} cells under row and site legality and a density target, and routing moves 10 5 10^{5} to 10 7 10^{7} nets over layers, tracks and vias under capacity and design rules, while the objectives widen along the flow from wirelength and outline area to congestion, timing, vias and overflow. They share one proxy objective, the half-perimeter wirelength (HPWL), the sum over nets of the half perimeter of the smallest box around the net’s pins, because the wires do not exist until routing; congestion and timing enter later ( Viswanathan et al., 2012 ) . The floorplan bounds all of it, since the relative position of the blocks fixes the length of the nets between them, the regions the router can use and the area of the die. Mixed-size placement handles macros and cells together with the macro shapes fixed ( Adya et al., 2004 ; Chen et al., 2008a ; Chen et al., 2008b ) , and macro placement, the task of the reinforcement learning line ( Mirhoseini et al., 2021 ) , is floorplanning with every shape fixed. Figure 8: Top: the three stages, drawn schematically: floorplanning arranges blocks and shapes the soft ones, placement fills rows with fixed-height cells around the macros, routing draws every net as wires on metal layers. Bottom: a 60-block validation case of FloorSet: the reference layout with its annotations, nets and outline pins, the raw sample of Trinity at NFE = 8 \mathrm{NFE}{=}8 with overlap in red, and the legalized sample, each with its overlap ratio and wirelength and area gaps.

sections.heading: A.2 What an Instance Contains
sections.text: A floorplanning instance is a netlist reduced to the block level. FloorSet gives for every case the target area of each block, the weighted nets between blocks, the pins on the die outline with their nets, the five kinds of annotation, and a reference layout ( Mallappa et al., 2024 ) ; Figure 8 (bottom left) draws one case. Over the 100 validation cases the instances span 21 to 120 blocks, a median of 70, with 29 to 7,056 nets between blocks and 50 to 466 pins on the outline. The annotations are not rare: a median case has 9% fixed-shape blocks, 4% pre-placed blocks, 31% of its blocks in one of three or four clusters, 8% in a multi-instance group and 35% of its blocks coded to a boundary, so most blocks carry a rule beyond non-overlap. Each stands for something a design team knows before the floorplan exists: a fixed shape is a hard macro delivered as a finished layout, a pre-placed block an interface or analog part whose position the package or an earlier floorplan settled, a cluster a functional unit or power domain whose blocks must stay close, a multi-instance group a block instantiated several times whose one internal layout is reused, and a boundary code a block that must reach the pins at the die edge. The reference layouts are tight, with 1 to 5% dead space, and Table 20 scores their residual violations. The hard cost of Eq. ( 1 ) follows a public floorplanning evaluation on this data; Appendix C states every rule as implemented.

sections.heading: A.3 What Makes It Hard
sections.text: Four things, and they compound. Packing: placing rectangles without overlap into the smallest outline is NP-hard even with fixed shapes and no nets, and the sequence pair alone encodes ( n ! ) 2 (n!)^{2} arrangements of n n blocks ( Murata et al., 1996 ; Kahng et al., 2011 ) . Shapes: a soft block adds a continuous choice to every combinatorial one, which has an exact solution on a slicing tree ( Stockmeyer, 1983 ) and none on a general topology. Coupling: wirelength pulls connected blocks together, non-overlap holds them apart, a cluster asks for adjacency, a boundary code for the edge, a fixed outline for a total that fits ( Adya and Markov, 2003 ) , all on the same coordinates, so a layout that satisfies the rules is in general not near one that scores well. The bottom row of Figure 8 shows the size of the effect: the raw sample overlaps 2.2% of its area with a wirelength 1.5% below the reference, and legalizing it removes every overlap by moving blocks until the wirelength is 0.5% and the area 1.1% below. Evaluation: feasibility is binary, so a layout with one thin overlap scores as infeasible although it is nearly done, and both an instance-level search and any comparison of intermediate layouts need a graded measure of the distance to feasible; annealers carry one in their cost, analytical placers in their density penalty, and Section 3.1 defines one for this paper. And the search repeats per instance, minutes to hours of annealing per floorplan, the motivation for parallel annealers ( Mostafa et al., 2024 ) and learned placers alike.

sections.heading: The constraints inside the search.
sections.text: In the 1980s floorplanning and cell placement were both done by simulated annealing ( Kirkpatrick et al., 1983 ; Sechen and Sangiovanni-Vincentelli, 1986 ) , floorplanning over slicing structures encoded as Polish expressions ( Otten, 1982 ; Wong and Liu, 1986 ) . What survived is the search in an encoding whose decode is overlap-free, so every move is judged on wirelength and area alone. What did not is the slicing restriction, which cannot express some tight packings. The 1990s produced non-slicing encodings with the same property, the sequence pair ( Murata et al., 1996 ) , the bounded-sliceline grid ( Nakatake et al., 1996 ) , the O-tree ( Guo et al., 1999 ) , the B ∗ -tree ( Chang et al., 2000 ) , the transitive closure graph ( Lin and Chang, 2001 ) and the corner block list ( Hong et al., 2000 ) , and extended the sequence pair to hard, soft and pre-placed modules through a linear program over positions ( Murata and Kuh, 1998 ) , the ancestor of the program in Appendix F . The 2000s made the outline a constraint to fit ( Adya and Markov, 2001 ; Adya and Markov, 2003 ) and put macros and cells into one problem ( Adya et al., 2004 ; Chen et al., 2008b ) , and PARSAC runs this line in parallel on the constraint family of FloorSet ( Mostafa et al., 2024 ) . Placement meanwhile left annealing, which does not scale past 10 5 10^{5} cells, for the analytical route ( Sigl et al., 1991 ) : minimize wirelength plus a differentiable penalty for overlap or density over continuous coordinates, then legalize. Quadratic placers ( Hall, 1970 ; Kleinhans et al., 1991 ; Viswanathan and Chu, 2005 ; Spindler et al., 2008b ) gave way to nonlinear ones ( Chen et al., 2008a ) and to the electrostatic density model ( Lu et al., 2015 ; Cheng et al., 2019 ) , with legalization a stage of its own ( Spindler et al., 2008a ) . What survived is the split into a graded relaxation and a legalizer, and DREAMPlace ran the relaxation in a deep learning framework on a GPU ( Lin et al., 2021 ) , the bridge to learned placers. Surveys of the two eras are Markov et al. (2015) and Huang et al. (2021) . Both branches meet the constraints and the objectives at every move, at the price of a search per netlist. Trinity keeps the graded energy of the analytical branch and moves it from that search into the training loss.

sections.heading: The constraints outside training.
sections.text: The 2020s brought learning and a debate about evidence. A graph network policy that places one macro per step, trained on a set of designs and fine-tuned on each new one ( Mirhoseini et al., 2021 ) , was re-run by an independent group against annealing and commercial tools, which questioned its margins ( Cheng et al., 2023 ; Markov, 2024 ) . The replies improved the representation and the search, with joint placement and routing ( Cheng and Yan, 2021 ) , visual states ( Lai et al., 2022 ) , offline decision transformers ( Lai et al., 2023 ) , tree and evolutionary search ( Geng et al., 2024 ; Deng et al., 2025 ) , cross-stage rewards ( Geng et al., 2025 ) , expert knowledge in the policy ( Gao et al., 2026 ) and black-box optimization with a wire mask in place of a policy ( Shi et al., 2023 ) , and they produced the shared data the debate had lacked: netlists with placement and routing labels ( Chai et al., 2022 ) , floorplans with design constraints ( Mallappa et al., 2024 ) , and benchmarks that score a placer by what the finished chip achieves or by a black-box protocol ( Wang et al., 2024 ; Xue et al., 2026 ) . Floorplanning with soft blocks entered through a graph convolutional policy ( Xu et al., 2022 ) , a corner-block-list representation learned across designs ( Amini et al., 2022 ) and direct regression of every position from the netlist graph ( Liu et al., 2023b ) . Across the line the shapes stay fixed and the constraints stay outside the function the model learns, and Appendix K.2 measures what the regressors’ conditional mean costs on our own backbone.

sections.heading: Generative placement and its corrections.
sections.text: The generative turn came from layout generation in graphics and architecture, where diffusion models draft documents and building floor plans under alignment and adjacency rules ( Inoue et al., 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2023 ; Shabani et al., 2023 ) , and from molecules and combinatorial problems ( Hoogeboom et al., 2022 ; Sun and Yang, 2023 ) , together with the toolkit those models use to satisfy rules at sampling time: gradient guidance ( Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021 ; Ho and Salimans, 2022 ) , posterior sampling under a measurement ( Chung et al., 2023 ) and constraint losses on the clean prediction ( Chen et al., 2024 ; Bastek et al., 2025 ) . The diffusion placers apply this toolkit to macro placement. ChipDiffusion ( Lee et al., 2025 ) , DiffPlace ( Trung and Hy, 2026 ) and MacroDiff+ ( Yoon et al., 2026 ) predict the noise and steer every denoising step with an overlap or wirelength gradient in the forms Table 38 lists, a heterogeneous graph variant follows the same design ( Zheng et al., 2025 ) , and FlowPlace ( Xie et al., 2026 ) predicts the velocity and projects each step onto a grid without overlap. All four train with a plain denoising loss, so the constraint terms appear first in the sampler and then in another form in a post-hoc loop, ten gradient steps in each of 1,000 denoising steps, up to 700 optimizer steps per denoising step, or 5,000 steps after sampling, before a legalizer closes what remains. They keep the learned proposal of the sequential line and the graded penalty of the analytical line but apply the penalty after the model, where the earlier eras had it inside the optimization, and their papers score the legalized endpoint at one sampling budget. Appendix J reproduces the three in-sampler corrections on our recipe, Section 4.3 the loops, and Appendix K shows how much of the difference between generators the legalizer hides. Trinity moves the penalty back into training and samples without guidance.

sections.heading: Objectives and conditioning.
sections.text: Noise prediction ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Nichol and Dhariwal, 2021 ; Salimans and Ho, 2022 ) , flow matching and rectified flow ( Lipman et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2023a ) and stochastic interpolants ( Ma et al., 2024 ) are linear transformations between data and noise, and a design-space view separates the prediction target, the time distribution and the weighting ( Karras et al., 2022 ) , the interface of Appendix B.1 . Following JiT ( Li and He, 2026 ) , Trinity predicts the clean layout and trains on the velocity it implies, the one output an energy can score, and LACE ( Chen et al., 2024 ) and physics-informed diffusion ( Bastek et al., 2025 ) supervise the same clean prediction with constraint losses in other domains. The backbone is a Diffusion Transformer ( Peebles and Xie, 2023 ) with the time step as a token ( Bao et al., 2023 ) , and the netlist enters it through an attention bias from the net incidence in the manner of Graphormer ( Ying et al., 2021 ) , a message-passing residual beside attention in the manner of GraphGPS ( Rampášek et al., 2022 ) , and a spectral positional encoding from the Laplacian eigenvectors ( Belkin and Niyogi, 2003 ; Dwivedi and Bresson, 2020 ; Kreuzer et al., 2021 ; Dwivedi et al., 2022 ; Dwivedi et al., 2023 ) .

sections.heading: A.5 The Benchmark Suites
sections.text: Table 11 lists the suites the field measures itself on. The floorplanning suites are small and old: MCNC ( Kozminski, 1991 ) has 9 to 49 blocks per instance and GSRC extends it to 300 soft blocks, the scale of Table 8 . The placement suites are large: the mixed-size suite ( Adya et al., 2004 ) and the ISPD contests of 2005 and 2006 ( Nam et al., 2005 ; Nam, 2006 ) fixed the form of an industrial placement benchmark, millions of cells, fixed macros, a fixed outline and a density target, and the DAC 2012 contest added routability ( Viswanathan et al., 2012 ) . Learning needs many instances rather than a few large ones, which CircuitNet supplies for placement and routing prediction ( Chai et al., 2022 ) and FloorSet for floorplanning, 996,000 synthetic training instances with the design constraints the older suites lack ( Mallappa et al., 2024 ) . sections.heading: Wire dropout.
sections.text: Three mixtures were trained on the plain base: a mild one (70% of instances untouched, 30% at a rate from Beta(1,3)), the adopted mixture (50% untouched, 40% Beta(1,3), 10% U(0.9,1)) and a heavy one (30% untouched, 50% Beta(1,2), 20% U(0.8,1)). On our 12,000 val set the adopted mixture is within ± 1 % \pm 1\% of the base on every soft metric except the immutable-block deviation ( − 20 % -20\% ) and the MIB variance ( − 16 % -16\% ), has the lowest soft cost of the set (2.092 against 2.106) and is the closest arm to the reference distribution on all four distances with p = 0.005 p=0.005 . The mild and the heavy mixture move the wirelength gap toward zero and the area gap up by 30 to 40%. The adopted mixture is the recipe of every model from the term ladders on.

sections.heading: B.3 Architecture Specification
sections.text: The backbone is a plain transformer with one token per block: 12 layers, width 768, 12 heads, RMSNorm, SwiGLU and QK-normalization. The input projection embeds the noisy latent z t , i z_{t,i} with 19 conditioning columns per block (area, kind, anchor value and mask, group identifiers, boundary code, pin pull). The time step enters as one prepended token in the manner of U-ViT ( Bao et al., 2023 ) , so the block has no adaptive normalization and the same block serves the deterministic regressors of Section 4.1 . Three components put the netlist into the network (Figure 2 ). The input projection is one linear layer from the concatenated 3 latent, 19 conditioning and 2 spectral coordinates, 24 in total, to the width of 768. Attention bias. The max-normalized log ⁡ ( 1 + A i ​ j ) \log(1+A_{ij}) is added to every attention logit through one learned gate ( Ying et al., 2021 ) ; padded keys receive a large negative bias, and the bias rides the mask argument of the fused attention kernel. Information mover. Every layer adds one graph-convolution hop behind a zero-initialized gate, x ← x + g ​ W ​ A ^ ​ x x\leftarrow x+g\,W\hat{A}x with A ^ = D − 1 ​ A \hat{A}=D^{-1}A the row-normalized netlist adjacency, so each block receives the mean of its neighbours ( Kipf and Welling, 2017 ; Rampášek et al., 2022 ) . The residual supplies one-hop netlist information in parallel with attention, the zero gate makes the layer a plain transformer layer at initialization, and it adds 7.1M parameters for 92.9M in total. Spectral positional encoding. Two input columns hold the second and third eigenvectors of the normalized netlist Laplacian, the quadratic-placement drawing of the netlist ( Hall, 1970 ; Kleinhans et al., 1991 ; Koren, 2003 ) , in the same ( c x / s , c y / s ) (c_{x}/s,c_{y}/s) frame the model generates. Sign and axis are fixed by unit norm and non-negative skewness, because a reflected drawing is a different layout.

sections.heading: B.4 The Ported Prior Arts
sections.text: Each port keeps the published network and objective, trains under Table 12 on the same data, consumes the same 3-D latent and the same 19 conditioning columns as our models, and samples with the same Euler integrator and the same overrides. FlowPlace and ChipDiffusion share the AttGNN network, three blocks of two GATv2 layers, an MLP, global attention and an MLP at hidden width 256 with FiLM time conditioning, 6.3M parameters; FlowPlace trains rectified flow with a velocity head and uniform t t and publishes no loop, ChipDiffusion trains a cosine DDPM with an ϵ \epsilon head and uniform t t and follows sampling with a 5,000-iteration gradient legalizer on legality and HPWL potentials, in its standard, scheduled and dual-ascent Adam variants. DiffPlace keeps VectorGNNV2Global, eight blocks of two vector message-passing layers with FiLM, a global supernode and hidden width 256, 23.9M parameters with the orientation head dropped, trains a linear- β \beta DDPM with an ϵ \epsilon head at T = 1,000 T{=}1{,}000 , and follows sampling with a 500-iteration gradient refinement. MacroDiff+ keeps its heterogeneous GATv2 cell and net network of five layers at width 64 with a 1-D token U-Net of widths 32 ⋅ [ 1 , 2 , 4 , 8 ] 32\cdot[1,2,4,8] , 5.0M parameters, trains a linear- β \beta DDPM at T = 200 T{=}200 whose ϵ \epsilon is composed as α ​ ( ∂ HPWL / ∂ x ) ⊤ ​ net + β ​ cell \alpha\,(\partial\mathrm{HPWL}/\partial x)^{\top}\,\mathrm{net}+\beta\,\mathrm{cell} from a net head and a cell head, and follows sampling with a 500-iteration Adam loop on HPWL and overlap. The post-hoc loops (Section 4.3 ) are ported with autograd at their published optimizers, schedules and iteration counts, act on positions only, and run on a canvas equal to the raw bounding box plus a 5% margin, which their die-boundary terms need to separate blocks. A canvas tuned per method and shape freedom are not granted: the released energies have no shape variable, and shape freedom after sampling is the refiner’s (Appendix E ). The corrections three of the placers apply inside their samplers are ported separately, on the same canvas, for Appendix J (Table 38 ).

sections.heading: Hard feasibility and the hard cost.
sections.text: A layout is feasible when no pair of boxes overlaps by more than 10 − 6 10^{-6} on both axes, every soft block keeps w ​ h wh within 1% of its target area, every fixed-shape block keeps its ( w , h ) (w,h) and every preplaced block keeps its ( x , y , w , h ) (x,y,w,h) . Let c p c_{p} be the number of edge-connected components among the members of cluster p p , where two boxes are connected when they share an edge segment of positive length, s q s_{q} the number of distinct shapes in MIB group q q after rounding to 10 − 4 10^{-4} , and B B the set of boundary-coded blocks with codes 1 left, 2 right, 4 top, 8 bottom and corners as sums. Then V group \displaystyle V_{\mathrm{group}} = ∑ p ( c p − 1 ) , V mib = ∑ q ( s q − 1 ) , \displaystyle=\sum_{p}(c_{p}-1),\qquad V_{\mathrm{mib}}=\sum_{q}(s_{q}-1), V bnd \displaystyle V_{\mathrm{bnd}} = ∑ i ∈ B 𝟙 ​ [ a required side of ​ i ​ is off its outline edge by more than ​ 10 − 6 ] , \displaystyle=\sum_{i\in B}\mathbb{1}\bigl[\text{a required side of }i\text{ is off its outline edge by more than }10^{-6}\bigr], (5) and V rel = ( V group + V mib + V bnd ) / N soft V_{\mathrm{rel}}=(V_{\mathrm{group}}+V_{\mathrm{mib}}+V_{\mathrm{bnd}})/N_{\mathrm{soft}} with N soft N_{\mathrm{soft}} the number of soft-constrained slots. HPWL \mathrm{HPWL} is the net-weighted sum of centroid-to-centroid Manhattan distances over block-to-block and pin-to-block nets, the area is that of the layout bounding box, and both gaps are the layout value minus the reference value over the reference value, clamped at zero. The hard-cost total over a case set is ∑ c e n c / 12 ​ Cost c / ∑ c e n c / 12 \sum_{c}e^{n_{c}/12}\,\mathrm{Cost}_{c}/\sum_{c}e^{n_{c}/12} ; the paper reports the per-case mean and median and gives the totals in Appendix K .

sections.heading: The soft metric vector.
sections.text: Every layout, raw, refined or legalized, is scored with the same columns, every length in units of s = ∑ i a i s=\sqrt{\sum_{i}a_{i}} : • overlap ratio : ∑ i < j \sum_{i<j} intersection area over ∑ i \sum_{i} block area; • compactness : bounding-box area over ∑ i \sum_{i} block area, at least 1; • normalized wirelength wl \mathrm{wl} : HPWL / ( s ⋅ ∑ net weights ) \mathrm{HPWL}/(s\cdot\sum\text{net weights}) ; • hpwl gap , area gap : the two relative gaps to the reference, signed; • boundary distance : mean over boundary-coded blocks of the distance from each required side to its outline edge; • group gap : mean over same-cluster pairs of the axis-wise gap to contact; • MIB variance : mean within-group variance of ( log ⁡ w , log ⁡ h ) (\log w,\log h) ; • fixed distance : mean over fixed and preplaced blocks of the shape deviation over a \sqrt{a} plus, for preplaced blocks, the center distance; • severities sev group \mathrm{sev}_{\mathrm{group}} , sev mib \mathrm{sev}_{\mathrm{mib}} , sev bnd \mathrm{sev}_{\mathrm{bnd}} : per soft slot tanh ⁡ ( d / τ ) \tanh(d/\tau) with d d the slot’s distance to satisfaction and τ = 0.01 , 0.05 , 0.01 \tau=0.01,0.05,0.01 , summed over slots; • sev rel \mathrm{sev}_{\mathrm{rel}} : ( sev group + sev mib + sev bnd ) / N soft (\mathrm{sev}_{\mathrm{group}}+\mathrm{sev}_{\mathrm{mib}}+\mathrm{sev}_{\mathrm{bnd}})/N_{\mathrm{soft}} , the severity analogue of V rel V_{\mathrm{rel}} ; • soft cost : the second aggregate of Eq. ( 1 ), computed per case before averaging. In every table the boundary distance, the group gap and the fixed distance are given in units of 10 − 3 10^{-3} , the MIB variance in units of 10 − 6 10^{-6} and MMD in units of 10 − 3 10^{-3} ; the other columns are unscaled. The severities grade how far a slot is off and never how many slots are off, so the soft vector is continuous in the layout, and a jitter of 0.2% of s s on a reference layout moves every soft column monotonically while the hard cost jumps to its violated value. Where a model’s mean soft cost overflows (a few cases with gaps in the tens, only for the regressors and for the one-step samples of the ϵ \epsilon -head models) the per-case median and 90th percentile are given.

sections.heading: C.1 Distribution Metrics
sections.text: The per-layout metrics above score one layout against its own constraints and its own reference. The distribution metrics ask a different question: whether the set of layouts a model draws looks like the set of reference layouts. Each layout is mapped to a fixed-length, permutation-invariant descriptor that is a plain function of its geometry, with no learned encoder, and two standard distances are taken between the descriptor cloud of a model (all draws of one run at one NFE \mathrm{NFE} , 48,000 rows) and the descriptor cloud of the 12,000 reference layouts.

sections.heading: Density descriptor.
sections.text: Let W W be a rasterization window and G G a grid size. In the bbox frame W W is the layout’s own bounding box, so the descriptor sees the arrangement of the blocks and factors out the size of the outline; in the fixed frame W W is the square of side 2 ​ s 2s centered on the bounding-box center, so the descriptor also sees how far the layout spreads in absolute units. W W is cut into G × G G\times G cells g g of equal size, and the coverage of cell g g by block i i is the fraction of the cell the box B i B_{i} occupies, c i ​ ( g ) = | B i ∩ g | | g | ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] . c_{i}(g)=\frac{|B_{i}\cap g|}{|g|}\in[0,1]. (6) Four fields are stacked: all blocks, soft blocks, fixed and preplaced blocks, and the net-weighted center density, f all ​ ( g ) \displaystyle f_{\mathrm{all}}(g) = ∑ i c i ​ ( g ) , f soft ​ ( g ) = ∑ i ​ soft c i ​ ( g ) , f lock ​ ( g ) = ∑ i ​ fixed , preplaced c i ​ ( g ) , \displaystyle=\sum_{i}c_{i}(g),\qquad f_{\mathrm{soft}}(g)=\sum_{i\ \mathrm{soft}}c_{i}(g),\qquad f_{\mathrm{lock}}(g)=\sum_{i\ \mathrm{fixed,\ preplaced}}c_{i}(g), f net ​ ( g ) \displaystyle f_{\mathrm{net}}(g) = ∑ i : center ⁡ ( i ) ∈ g ω i ∑ i ω i , \displaystyle=\frac{\sum_{i:\,\mathrm{center}(i)\in g}\omega_{i}}{\sum_{i}\omega_{i}}, (7) where ω i \omega_{i} is the total weight of the nets incident on block i i (block-to-block weights counted at both endpoints, pin weights at the block). The coverage fields sum above 1 1 in a cell where blocks overlap, so the descriptor sees overlap as well as arrangement. The descriptor ϕ G ​ ( layout ) ∈ ℝ 4 ​ G 2 \phi_{G}(\text{layout})\in\mathbb{R}^{4G^{2}} is the concatenation of the four fields: 256 dimensions at G = 8 G=8 and 576 at G = 12 G=12 . FLD8b, FLD8f, FLD12b and FLD12f name the Fréchet distance below on ϕ 8 \phi_{8} and ϕ 12 \phi_{12} in the two frames.

sections.heading: Position descriptor.
sections.text: The block centers c i c_{i} are scaled by s s and shifted by the bounding-box center. The descriptor collects the biased covariance of the center cloud ( Σ x ​ x , Σ y ​ y , Σ x ​ y \Sigma_{xx},\Sigma_{yy},\Sigma_{xy} ), the per-axis skewness and excess kurtosis of the standardized coordinates, the radius of gyration mean i ​ ‖ c i ‖ 2 \sqrt{\mathrm{mean}_{i}\,\|c_{i}\|^{2}} , a 16-bin histogram of the nearest-neighbor center distance on [ 0 , 0.5 ] [0,0.5] and a 16-bin histogram of the pairwise center distance on [ 0 , 2 ] [0,2] , both normalized to sum to one: 8 + 16 + 16 = 40 8+16+16=40 dimensions. FPD names the Fréchet distance on it.

sections.heading: Fréchet distance.
sections.text: For a model cloud X X and the reference cloud R R with means μ X , μ R \mu_{X},\mu_{R} and sample covariances Σ X , Σ R \Sigma_{X},\Sigma_{R} (each with 10 − 6 ​ I 10^{-6}I added for the matrix square root), d F 2 ​ ( X , R ) = ‖ μ X − μ R ‖ 2 2 + Tr ⁡ ( Σ X + Σ R − 2 ​ ( Σ X ​ Σ R ) 1 / 2 ) , d_{\mathrm{F}}^{2}(X,R)=\|\mu_{X}-\mu_{R}\|_{2}^{2}+\operatorname{Tr}\!\bigl(\Sigma_{X}+\Sigma_{R}-2\,(\Sigma_{X}\Sigma_{R})^{1/2}\bigr), (8) the squared Wasserstein-2 distance between the Gaussian fits of the two clouds, the form used by FID ( Heusel et al., 2017 ) . The mean term and the covariance term are stored separately in the result files of the supplementary material. The distance is computed on the full clouds, uses the first two moments only, and is not standardized, so cells with a large natural variance weigh more.

sections.heading: Kernel MMD.
sections.text: For the G = 8 G=8 bbox descriptor every dimension is first standardized by the reference standard deviation, ϕ ~ = ϕ / ( σ R + 10 − 9 ) \tilde{\phi}=\phi/(\sigma_{R}+10^{-9}) , so every cell weighs the same. With the Gaussian kernel k ( x , y ) = exp ( − ∥ x − y ∥ 2 / 2 h 2 ) k(x,y)=\exp(-\|x-y\|^{2}/2h^{2}) and the bandwidth h h set to the median pairwise Euclidean distance within a 4,000-row subsample of the standardized reference, the unbiased estimator ( Gretton et al., 2012 ) on subsamples X = { x i } i = 1 n X=\{x_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n} and R = { r j } j = 1 m R=\{r_{j}\}_{j=1}^{m} of 4,000 rows each is MMD u 2 ​ ( X , R ) = 1 n ⁡ ( n − 1 ) ​ ∑ i ≠ i ′ k ⁡ ( x i , x i ′ ) + 1 m ⁡ ( m − 1 ) ​ ∑ j ≠ j ′ k ⁡ ( r j , r j ′ ) − 2 n ​ m ​ ∑ i , j k ⁡ ( x i , r j ) . \mathrm{MMD}^{2}_{u}(X,R)=\frac{1}{n(n-1)}\sum_{i\neq i^{\prime}}k(x_{i},x_{i^{\prime}})+\frac{1}{m(m-1)}\sum_{j\neq j^{\prime}}k(r_{j},r_{j^{\prime}})-\frac{2}{nm}\sum_{i,j}k(x_{i},r_{j}). (9) This is MMD8b. The Gaussian kernel is characteristic, so the population MMD is zero only when the two distributions coincide and it is sensitive to every moment, which complements the two-moment Fréchet distance; in every table of the paper the two rank the models the same way. The estimate depends on the 4,000-row subsample, so the same run re-evaluated in another batch moves by a few percent: Trinity reads 2.5 in the batch of Table 1 and 2.3 in the seed batch of Appendix M . Every table prints the batch its rows were evaluated in, and a comparison is always read within one batch.

sections.heading: Permutation test.
sections.text: Whether a model A A is closer to the reference than a control B B is decided by a one-sided label-permutation test on MMD8b. With 2,000-row subsamples of A A , B B and R R the statistic is T = MMD u 2 ​ ( A , R ) − MMD u 2 ​ ( B , R ) T=\mathrm{MMD}^{2}_{u}(A,R)-\mathrm{MMD}^{2}_{u}(B,R) ; under the null that A A and B B are exchangeable the pooled rows are relabeled at random 200 times, giving T 1 , … , T 200 T_{1},\dots,T_{200} , and p = 1 + # ⁡ { ℓ : T ℓ ≤ T } 1 + 200 . p=\frac{1+\#\{\ell:T_{\ell}\leq T\}}{1+200}. (10) A small p p means the observed difference is farther below zero than a random relabeling produces, so A A is closer to the reference than B B ; p = 1 / 201 ≈ 0.005 p=1/201\approx 0.005 is the floor. The same model with another training seed tests at p = 0.20 p=0.20 to 1.00 1.00 against the original (Appendix M ), the null band of the test.

sections.heading: Reading the distribution metrics.
sections.text: Lower is closer to the reference distribution, which is fidelity to the training layouts, not cost: the reference layouts leave 9.1% of the boundary-coded blocks off their edge, so a model that places more coded blocks on the edge moves away from the reference in the cells along the outline, which is why the boundary term at high weight and Trinity’s own FLD8f can rise while every per-layout metric improves. The bbox frame answers "is the arrangement right", the fixed frame "is the spread right", the position descriptor "is the center cloud right", and the four together are read as a set. The main text writes FLD for FLD8b and MMD for MMD8b.

sections.heading: Correlation measures.
sections.text: Per ( NFE , steps ) (\mathrm{NFE},\text{steps}) cell of a line, the Spearman ρ \rho and Kendall τ \tau of the per-draw soft cost against the per-draw hard cost over the 48,000 draws and over the 12,000 per-case means, Pearson r r and R 2 R^{2} on raw and on log values, and the Spearman per soft column. Across a grid, the same measures on the cell means. Pooled, over every draw of a line and over the eight lines together.

sections.heading: A property of the data set.
sections.text: The reference layouts satisfy every cluster abutment. They leave 9.1% of the boundary-coded blocks off their required edge and pay about 10% in hard cost for it. The six quantities read the constraint annotations and never the reference layout, so a model trained with them can place a coded block on its edge where the reference does not, and Trinity’s boundary distance is one quarter of the plain control’s.

sections.heading: D.5 What Is Predicted and What Is Measured
sections.text: Two limits remain. Training with the terms does not sample the reweighted law of Corollary D.1 either; the claim is asymmetric, the loop’s clean-space gradient missing the exact guidance of Lemma D.2 by an amount Σ 0 | t \Sigma_{0|t} does not control, while Theorem D.1 characterizes the trained head exactly at no sampling cost. The results concern where a correction is applied, not whether the six quantities are right, which Section 4.2 measures.

sections.text: Adam with β 1 = 0 \beta_{1}=0 : v ← β 2 ​ v + ( 1 − β 2 ) ​ g 2 v\leftarrow\beta_{2}v+(1-\beta_{2})g^{2} , z ← z − lr t ​ g / ( v / ( 1 − β 2 t ) + ϵ ) z\leftarrow z-\mathrm{lr}_{t}\,g/(\sqrt{v/(1-\beta_{2}^{t})}+\epsilon) . Without momentum a block that has just been pushed out of an overlap stops when the force stops instead of coasting into the next block, and the per-coordinate normalization lets each term move its block at the full step whatever its magnitude, so the weights set the priority where terms compete on one coordinate. The learning-rate vector is precomputed from the schedule, the overrides are re-applied after every step, and K K steps run inside one compiled function. At 400 steps the refiner takes about one millisecond per layout: 2.6 μ \mu s per step per layout with 1,000 layouts in a batch on one RTX 5090, wall-clock with the device synchronized, the median of five timed repeats after a warm-up (Table 10 ), and 20 ms per layout at 32 per batch.

sections.heading: Appendix F The Legalizer
sections.text: Legalization reads a sequence-pair relation for every pair of blocks from the refined layout (the axis of least penetration, ordered by center) and solves one linear program that packs the blocks under those relations with preplaced blocks pinned, cluster members abutting along a spanning tree and boundary-coded edges on the outline, minimizing the outline plus the displacement from the refined positions ( Murata et al., 1996 ; Murata and Kuh, 1998 ) . When the program is infeasible the soft terms become penalties and the relations of the conflicting preplaced pairs are flipped. A second program then lets soft blocks change aspect at fixed area under the same relations, kept when the checker scores it better, and the smallest uniform expansion that separates every pair is reported as the price of residual overlap. Table 18 lists the eight steps. Table 18: The legalizer, one stage of eight steps. Every step is a one-line rule or a standard constraint-graph method; the program of step E and the knobs are below. Step Rule Kind A anchors pre-placed blocks to their target box, fixed blocks to their shape, soft blocks to their exact area, an all-soft MIB group to one shape rule B expansion every free block moved outward from the layout centre by the smallest λ ≥ 1 \lambda\geq 1 (cap 10) at which no pair overlaps; λ \lambda recorded per draw rule C relations per pair, the axis of larger separation (least penetration if overlapping) and the order along it, read from the unexpanded layout sequence pair ( Murata et al., 1996 ) , TCG ( Lin and Chang, 2001 ) C ′ rewrites a block ordered between an abutting pair, or outside a coded block on its coded side, re-ordered on the other axis; pinned pairs never rewritten rule D abutment tree per cluster a spanning tree over member pairs ranked by gap, missing perpendicular overlap, blocks in between and pre-placed collisions rule E packing LP one linear program over positions at fixed shapes LP packing with pre-placed modules ( Murata and Kuh, 1998 ) F ladder on infeasibility: abutment and boundary as penalties, then the violated pinned relations flipped (six rounds), then every free block above the pre-placed ones rule G contact snap tree pairs within 10 − 6 10^{-6} of contact set to exact contact, overlap-checked rule H aspect pass one more program with every soft non-MIB shape free within 1.3 per side at fixed area, kept when the checker scores it feasible and cheaper sequential LP

sections.text: Variables: X i , Y i X_{i},Y_{i} for every block (fixed to the target for preplaced blocks), the outline L , R , B , T L,R,B,T , and non-negative auxiliaries for absolute values and slacks. Objective, minimized: ( R − L ) ​ H 0 / A 0 + ( T − B ) ​ W 0 / A 0 (R-L)\,H_{0}/A_{0}+(T-B)\,W_{0}/A_{0} (the outline, linearized at the input bounding box W 0 × H 0 = A 0 W_{0}\times H_{0}=A_{0} ) + μ / ( n s ) ∑ i ( | X i − x ^ i | + | Y i − y ^ i | ) +\ \mu/(ns)\sum_{i}(|X_{i}-\hat{x}_{i}|+|Y_{i}-\hat{y}_{i}|) (displacement from the restored positions) + ( penalty / s ) × +\ (\text{penalty}/s)\times soft slacks + ( 1,000 / s ) × +\ (1{,}000/s)\times probe slacks. Size: n 2 / 2 n^{2}/2 relation rows plus O ⁡ ( n ) O(n) others, at most about 7,200 rows at n = 120 n=120 ; one solve takes a few to about 50 milliseconds, and a draw takes 240 to 300 milliseconds end to end including every ladder rung it needs, of which the solver is 87 to 99 milliseconds.

sections.heading: The ladder (step F).
sections.text: The program of step E runs first with the abutment and boundary constraints hard, then with them as penalties, and when that program is infeasible the flip loop runs at most six rounds of two programs each. The first is a probe: the relation of every free and pre-placed pair carries a probe slack, and the pairs whose slack the solution uses are the pinned relations the layout cannot hold. The second is the packing program with those relations moved to the other axis, ordered as the probe placed the two blocks, and every pinned relation hard again. A packing program that places without overlap ends the loop with its layout. When the six rounds are spent, or a probe is infeasible or uses no slack, the flipped relations are discarded and only the pre-placed blocks of the pairs the probes flagged are kept: the next rung reads the relations from the layout again, without the rewrites of step C ′ , and orders every free block above each of those blocks, and the last rung orders every free block above every pre-placed block, which is feasible by construction.

sections.heading: The snap (step G).
sections.text: The snap is a gate on single-block moves. For every tree pair whose gap is within 10 − 6 10^{-6} of contact, the checker’s tolerance, the later block along the pair’s axis is moved onto the edge of the earlier one, and the move is kept only when the moved block overlaps no other block, over at most three sweeps of the pairs or until a sweep keeps no move. The layout enters feasible, each kept move displaces one block by at most that tolerance and is admitted only when the block overlaps none of the others, and no shape or other pair changes, so the layout is feasible after every kept move and at exit.

sections.heading: Residual analysis.
sections.text: On the 240-case tuning subset at 400 refiner steps, before the aspect pass, the hard program is feasible on 24% of draws at cost 1.02, the penalized program on 57% at 1.2, pinned flips on 15%, and the last rungs on 4% at about 3. The residual violations of the penalized rung on 80 draws are 95 boundary counts (14 on preplaced blocks, 20 with a preplaced block already beyond the coded edge, 38 corner codes, 69 within 2% of s s of the edge) and 142 cluster counts (10 with a preplaced member, 133 with the nearest member within 2% of s s ), near-misses a position-only program under fixed relations cannot close, which is what the aspect pass addresses: with it, the counted violations per draw fall from 1.4 + 1.5 1.4+1.5 to 1.0 + 1.2 1.0+1.2 , the area gap from + 0.117 +0.117 to + 0.081 +0.081 , and the best-of-4 cost from 1.103 to 1.066.

sections.text: Three of the four ported placers also correct the sample inside their samplers, and the generator comparison of Section 4.2 leaves those corrections out so that every network meets the same Euler sampler. ChipDiffusion, DiffPlace and MacroDiff+ are sampled with the guidance their released code applies at every step, ported onto our sampler as Table 38 describes, on the 12,000 val set at NFE ∈ { 1 , 2 , 4 , 8 , 16 , 32 } \mathrm{NFE}\in\{1,2,4,8,16,32\} with four draws from the noise of their free shards, so that every guided draw pairs with a free one. FlowPlace’s in-sampler step is a projection onto the hard constraints that its own evaluation configuration disables, and it is not reproduced. The guided samples are scored on the fifteen soft columns, refined by the closed-form refiner on the reduced grid of Appendix I.2 , passed through the three ported loops at NFE = 32 \mathrm{NFE}{=}32 , and measured against the reference distribution as in Appendix C . The legalizer is not run on them. DiffPlace’s released update raises overlap. Its overlap loss is the positive pairwise overlap area and its sampler subtracts the loss gradient from the predicted noise, which moves the implied clean sample up that gradient. The port runs the released sign as the reproduction and a reference arm with the sign flipped, whose per-block normalization still pushes every overlapping block by the same 0.03 ​ λ t 0.03\,\lambda_{t} whatever its overlap. sections.heading: J.3 Distance to the Reference
sections.text: Table 42 measures the guided samples against the reference distribution. At NFE = 32 \mathrm{NFE}{=}32 every guidance moves its placer away from it, FLD8b by seven to eleven times (ChipDiffusion 0.273 to 3.10, DiffPlace 2.86 to 19.7, MacroDiff+ 0.624 to 4.36) and MMD8b by two to sixteen times, and no guided run is closer to the reference than the plain control ( p = 1.00 p=1.00 ). At NFE = 1 \mathrm{NFE}{=}1 the guided and the free samples sit at the same distance (FLD8b 92 to 102), where the one-step draw dominates whatever the guidance adds. The three corrections move the sample along the terms they model, overlap and wirelength, and away from the reference layouts on every term they do not, which is the pattern the ported loops show on the reference layouts in Appendix G . Measured at the stage where the guidance acts, the trade is visible in the columns of Table 39 . After the legalizer, which removes the overlap on every arm, the same trade would appear as a few percent of area and wirelength with no column to name it.

sections.heading: Appendix L Classical Floorplanners
sections.text: The full pipeline of Trinity meets the classical floorplanners on two protocols: the FloorSet val set under the contest cost, and the soft-block benchmarks on which the prior work reports its numbers. The pipeline is always the same: Trinity samples at NFE = 8 \mathrm{NFE}{=}8 , the closed-form refiner runs 400 steps, the legalizer closes every draw on 16 CPU workers and the cheapest feasible draw is kept. Every number is the legalized layout’s, and every timed run had the machine to itself.

sections.heading: The classical lines.
sections.text: PARSAC ( Mostafa et al., 2024 ) is the constraints-aware B*-tree annealer of the group that built FloorSet. We load its C++ engine as released and run its published schedule of 100 stages from a random tree, with the boundary codes, clusters, fixed and preplaced blocks and MIB shapes of each case mapped one to one, for 10 7 10^{7} steps per worker, its budget in the paper. A worker is one independent run on one CPU core, and the best of k k workers is the per-case minimum over k k runs at k k times the CPU time. Every run is snapshotted after each stage and every snapshot is legalized and scored, so the curves below are one worker’s best legalized cost so far against its own elapsed seconds. The sequence-pair annealer is the one of BBOPlace-Bench ( Xue et al., 2026 ) with 10 5 10^{5} cost evaluations, and Astra is the public contest solver, whose published layouts we re-score with our checker and which reproduce its own numbers.

sections.heading: Continuing from the pipeline.
sections.text: PARSAC started from the tree of the pipeline’s legalized layout does not improve on it (the dashed line of Figure 18 ). The first snapshot after 10 4 10^{4} steps is already at a mean of 2.05 against the pipeline’s 1.019, and 10 6 10^{6} steps bring it back only to 1.31. A step-by-step probe of the hand-over on eight cases places the loss before any annealing: the compaction into a B*-tree moves 15 to 26 blocks, the tree does not reproduce the compacted layout on six of the eight cases, and the first greedy moves in PARSAC’s own cost, which weighs white space and normalized wirelength rather than the contest cost, raise the contest cost further. A continuation that helps would need the legalized layout’s exact representation and the contest cost as its acceptance rule.

sections.heading: N.8 Qualitative Examples
sections.text: Figure 60 follows three FloorSet val set cases through the pipeline of Section 4.4 at the setting of Table 8 : Trinity samples 48 draws at NFE = 8 \mathrm{NFE}{=}8 , the closed-form refiner runs 400 steps, the legalizer closes every draw, and the draw with the cheapest legalized layout is shown at every stage. The raw sample already has the outline, the boundary-coded blocks on their edges and the clusters together, with thin overlaps between neighbours; the refiner removes the overlaps and the legalizer packs the result. The gaps under the panels are signed, so a refined layout smaller than the reference, as on the 21-block case with an area gap of − 0.021 -0.021 , is visible where the hard cost would clamp it to zero. The best of 48 lands at a hard cost of 1.000, 1.000 and 1.074 against 1.091, 1.000 and 1.127 for the reference layouts of the 21-, 60- and 120-block cases, and every one of the 144 legalized draws is feasible. Figure 60: Three FloorSet val set cases with 21, 60 and 120 blocks through the pipeline, 48 draws at NFE = 8 \mathrm{NFE}{=}8 with 400 refiner steps and the shared legalizer, the draw with the cheapest legalized layout shown at every stage: the reference layout, the raw sample, the refined layout and the legalized layout. Blocks are coloured by constraint kind, every pairwise overlap region is red, block-to-block nets are faint lines between block centres, pins are dots on the outline with faint lines to their blocks, and the dashed box is the bounding outline. Under each panel: the signed area gap and HPWL gap to the reference, the severity sev rel \mathrm{sev}_{\mathrm{rel}} and the overlap ratio of the soft vector of Appendix C , which unlike the hard cost keep a layout smaller or shorter than the reference visible. Figure 61: Every generator on one 60-block FloorSet val set case from the same noise: the reference layout and the first draw of each line at NFE = 8 \mathrm{NFE}{=}8 , before any refinement. Colours as in Figure 60 . Under each panel, the overlap ratio and the soft cost of that layout. Figure 62: A 120-block case under the protocol of Figure 61 , with one region magnified. The window is placed on the largest overlap of the worst line and is the same in all three columns. Figure 61 puts the generators side by side on one of those cases. Because the sampler draws its noise from the case alone, the first draw of every line starts from one noise tensor, so the panels are paired rather than merely comparable. The ordering of Table 3 is visible block by block. On the case shown Trinity overlaps 0.022 of the block area at a soft cost of 1.44, FlowPlace and ChipDiffusion 0.058 and 0.054 at 3.24 and 3.55, and MacroDiff+ and DiffPlace 0.092 and 0.111 at 7.57 and 8.43; over the 21-, 60- and 120-block cases the same draw gives 0.014 to 0.022 for Trinity, 0.036 to 0.067 for the two velocity and cosine heads and 0.068 to 0.111 for the two remaining lines. The kind of failure also differs. Every line finds the outline and puts the boundary-coded blocks on their edges, so the gap is not in the global arrangement but in the local packing, which Figure 62 magnifies on a larger case: Trinity leaves thin contacts where a neighbour is a few thousandths of the layout scale too wide, while DiffPlace leaves whole blocks lying across one another. This is the defect the closed-form refiner of Section 4.3 removes in ten steps on Trinity and cannot remove on the prior arts in four hundred.
