sections.heading: Setup.
sections.text: Two variables define a rung of Trinity recipe: the hidden width d d and the layer count L L (Table 64 ). The width rungs fix L = 12 L=12 and vary d d , the depth rungs fix d = 768 d=768 and vary L L , and one rung sits off both axes at width 512 with 16 layers; the head dimension is 64 throughout, so the head count follows d d . The spectral positional encoding, the information mover, all six terms at λ = 0.01 \lambda{=}0.01 , the wire-dropout mixture and the frozen training recipe of Appendix B.2 (AdamW at a peak learning rate of 2 × 10 − 4 2\times 10^{-4} with cosine decay, effective batch 256, 200,000 steps, one GPU) are identical on every rung, so the runs differ in d d and L L alone. The width rungs sit at the sizes of the ported prior arts, 5.9M to 42.1M parameters against 5.0M to 23.9M for their networks; the depth rungs span 31.5M to 62.2M, so the two axes overlap in parameter count and separate the effect of the shape from that of the size. Every rung of the first six goes through the standard evaluation: our 12,000 val set at NFE ∈ { 1 , 2 , 4 , 8 , 16 , 32 } \mathrm{NFE}\in\{1,2,4,8,16,32\} with four draws and the fifteen soft columns, the distribution metrics at NFE = 1 \mathrm{NFE}{=}1 and 32 against the plain control with 200 permutations, the full NFE × \mathrm{NFE}\times steps refiner grid of Appendix I , and the same grid through the legalizer with the first draw and the best of four, as in Appendix K . The two rungs trained last, 192 / 12 at 5.9M parameters and 512 / 16 at 56.0M, have the raw scores of the val set only and appear in Tables 64 and 65 .

sections.heading: Width rungs, raw samples.
sections.text: Table 65 and Figure 63 give the widths at L = 12 L=12 on our 12,000 val set, the figure the four with full grids. At width 512, with 45% of Trinity’s parameters, the recipe reproduces Trinity within its seed spread on the raw sample (soft cost 1.534 against 1.514, 1.2 seed standard deviations; overlap within 0.5) and is equal to it at NFE = 1 \mathrm{NFE}{=}1 ; on the distribution metrics it is at or below Trinity at both NFE \mathrm{NFE} (FLD 0.0416 against 0.0423, MMD 0.0020 against 0.0025). Every rung is closer to the reference than the plain control at both NFE \mathrm{NFE} with p = 0.005 p=0.005 , every rung keeps the constraint level the terms train (boundary distance 0.86 to 0.97 × 10 − 3 0.97\times 10^{-3} against 3.0 × 10 − 3 3.0\times 10^{-3} for Trinity at λ = 0 \lambda{=}0 , MIB variance 2 to 4 × 10 − 6 4\times 10^{-6} against 6.7 × 10 − 6 6.7\times 10^{-6} ), and every rung improves the deviation of fixed and preplaced blocks over Trinity. Widths 384 and 256 give back overlap (23% and 32% more at NFE = 32 \mathrm{NFE}{=}32 ) and soft cost (1.612 and 1.703), width 256 also on the cluster gap and the boundary distance, and the rung at 10.6M parameters still stands at a soft cost of 1.70 against 2.46 for FlowPlace at 6.3M and 6.23 for DiffPlace at 23.9M under the same recipe and steps. Width 192 at 5.9M parameters, the size of the smallest ported network, continues the ladder to a soft cost of 1.827 at NFE = 32 \mathrm{NFE}{=}32 and 1.903 at NFE = 1 \mathrm{NFE}{=}1 with an overlap of 0.0347, the boundary distance and the MIB variance at 1.0 × 10 − 3 1.0\times 10^{-3} and 13.8 × 10 − 6 13.8\times 10^{-6} , and it stays below every ported placer’s soft cost at the same NFE \mathrm{NFE} . The shape of the NFE \mathrm{NFE} curve is the same at every width.

sections.heading: Depth rungs, raw samples.
sections.text: The depth rungs keep the width at 768 and remove layers (Table 65 , Figure 64 ). Every depth rung is behind Trinity on every constraint column at NFE = 32 \mathrm{NFE}{=}32 : at L = 8 L=8 the overlap is 6% higher, the boundary distance 17%, the cluster gap 11% and the MIB variance 2.2 times, for a soft cost of 1.593 against 1.514; at L = 6 L=6 the overlap is 37% higher and the soft cost 1.733; at L = 4 L=4 the overlap doubles to 0.048, FlowPlace’s level, the MIB variance is 3.9 times Trinity’s and the soft cost is 2.128. Depth costs more than width per parameter, and depth beyond twelve layers buys little: width 512 with 16 layers (56.0M) sits between 512 / 12 and Trinity at every NFE \mathrm{NFE} , 1.530 against 1.534 and 1.514 at NFE = 32 \mathrm{NFE}{=}32 and 1.679 against 1.682 and 1.679 at NFE = 1 \mathrm{NFE}{=}1 , with the overlap of 512 / 12 (0.0226) and the boundary distance and MIB variance of the width rungs, so four more layers at width 512 are worth 0.004 in soft cost for 14M parameters. By soft cost at NFE = 32 \mathrm{NFE}{=}32 the family orders as 768 / 12 (1.514), 512 / 16 (1.530), 512 / 12 (1.534), 768 / 8 (1.593), 384 / 12 (1.612), 256 / 12 (1.703), 768 / 6 (1.733), 192 / 12 (1.827) and 768 / 4 (2.128), so the 8-layer model at 62.2M parameters is within 0.02 of the width-384 model at 23.3M (and behind it after the refiner, 1.067 against 1.065, and on both distribution distances), the 6- and 4-layer models at 46.8M and 31.5M below the width-256 model at 10.6M, the 4-layer model below width 192 at 5.9M, and the loss per removed layer grows, + 0.08 +0.08 from 12 to 8 layers, + 0.14 +0.14 from 8 to 6 and + 0.39 +0.39 from 6 to 4. The deviation of fixed blocks is the one column that does not follow the depth. On the distribution metrics the 8- and 6-layer rungs are closer to the reference than the plain control at both NFE \mathrm{NFE} with p = 0.005 p=0.005 and inside Trinity’s seed band on FLD, while the 4-layer rung is not ( p = 1.000 p=1.000 at NFE = 32 \mathrm{NFE}{=}32 , FLD 0.151 against 0.103 for the plain control): it is the one rung of the study whose layouts are farther from the reference distribution than the plain control’s while its soft cost is lower. The reading is that the graph-convolution residual needs depth. The information mover moves information along the netlist one hop per layer, so a 4-layer model cannot carry the netlist far enough to place its blocks, while a narrow model at 12 layers still can. sections.heading: Scope.
sections.text: Every result is on FloorSet at 21 to 120 blocks with its synthetic constraint statistics, in the MIB-consistent variant of the data. The reference layouts leave 9.1% of the boundary-coded blocks off their edge, which bounds what a reference-matching metric can say about that constraint; the soft metrics read the constraint annotations instead, and the hard cost counts the violation, so the two costs of Section 3.1 are the right instruments for it.

sections.heading: Prior arts.
sections.text: The four diffusion placers are their published networks and objectives ported into the FloorSet vocabulary and trained under our recipe; their post-hoc loops are ported at their published settings, and their own legalizers are outside the study. This is the comparison that isolates the generator and the refiner, and it measures what a position-only design leaves on the table on a floorplanning task. Reproducing their published numbers on their own benchmarks was not part of this work.

sections.heading: Model size.
sections.text: Trinity has 92.9M parameters against 5 to 24M for the ported networks. Sampling is 0.02 to 0.32 seconds of the 0.5 to 1.9 seconds per case, so the size does not appear in the time budget, and FlowPlace’s own objective on our 85.8M backbone lands at a soft cost of 2.60 against 2.46 for its 6.3M network, which places the gap in the objective and the physics rather than in the parameter count. The size study of Appendix O trains Trinity recipe at widths d = 512 d=512 , 384, 256 and 192 with L = 12 L=12 layers (42.1M, 23.3M, 10.6M and 5.9M parameters, the sizes of the ported networks), at L = 8 L=8 , 6 and 4 layers with d = 768 d=768 (62.2M, 46.8M and 31.5M) and at width 512 with 16 layers (56.0M) under one learning rate: width 512 reproduces Trinity within its seed spread and four more layers on it add 0.004, the two smaller widths give back part of the overlap and soft cost on the raw sample while staying far ahead of the prior arts, and the refiner closes most of the remaining gap. Depth matters more than width: the 8-layer model at 62.2M parameters is within 0.02 of the 23.3M model of width 384 on the raw soft cost and behind it after the refiner and on both distribution distances, and the 4-layer model is the one rung whose layouts are farther from the reference distribution than the plain control’s. The information mover, a one-hop graph-convolution residual, moves information along the netlist one hop per layer, so a shallow model cannot carry the netlist far enough to place its blocks.

sections.heading: Seeds.
sections.text: Three seeds cover Trinity, Trinity at λ = 0 \lambda{=}0 , the plain control and FlowPlace; every other arm is a single run. A sweep-set delta under 2 to 3% on a constraint column or 1% on the soft cost is within one seed std of its control, and the claims of the paper are 17 to 70 std wide.

sections.heading: The legalizer.
sections.text: The legalizer is a fixed, minimal stage so that every comparison stays about the generator and the refiner. Its expansion step prices residual overlap in outline area, and after legalization Trinity still carries an area gap of 10% and a V rel V_{\mathrm{rel}} of 0.04 that best-of- N N recovers; a legalizer designed for numerically generated layouts, with wirelength in its objective, is the natural next stage of the pipeline and is future work.

sections.heading: Future work.
sections.text: Beyond the legalizer: the soft cost as a training signal for the sampler itself, distillation of the one-step model to remove the refiner from the time budget, and interactive use, where a designer edits one constraint and expects a local change; the overrides make that possible and it has not been evaluated.

sections.heading: Appendix Q Broader Impact
sections.text: Trinity is a physical-design study. Its positive impact is methodological: a way to write the constraints of a layout problem once and reuse them across training, refinement and evaluation, a generator that reaches a usable layout in one sampler step, and a three-stage evaluation that turns a discrete final score into a continuous development signal. Each of these transfers to other layout problems with hard rules and continuous objectives. The pipeline introduces no data set of proprietary designs: it trains on FloorSet’s synthetic layouts and evaluates on the public FloorSet validation set. A learned placer is used behind a verifying legalizer and a design-rule check, as it is here, and we see no misuse risk specific to this work beyond those shared by any design-automation tool.

sections.heading: Data.
sections.text: FloorSet ( Mallappa et al., 2024 ) is released by Intel Labs and distributed through HuggingFace under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 license (CC BY 4.0). 1 1 1 https://huggingface.co/datasets/IntelLabs/FloorSet We use the Lite training set and the 100-case validation set, transcoded into a columnar store without modification of content. In the raw Lite training set 99.25% of MIB groups have members with different ( w , h ) (w,h) , which makes every MIB loss and metric ill-defined; the variant used throughout sets each such group to one shape, and every model of the paper, the prior arts included, trains and is scored on it. The 100 validation cases carry consistent MIB annotations as released, 2 2 2 https://github.com/IntelLabs/FloorSet/issues/12 so they are used unchanged. No proprietary design data is used at any stage.

sections.heading: Code and models.
sections.text: The prior arts are ported from their public repositories into one codebase; their weights are not reused. The annealer follows BBOPlace-Bench at its published constants ( Xue et al., 2026 ) .

sections.heading: Supplementary material.
sections.text: The supplementary material is the code needed to reproduce training, sampling, refinement, legalization and scoring: the solver-agnostic domain library (data, scoring, legalization), the generator library (framings, the six terms, the backbone, the sampler, the refiner), the ported prior arts, the configuration file of every trained arm, refiner sweep and legalizer run, and the scripts that print every table of this paper from what a run writes. It carries no weights, no data and no result files, and a run reproduces the numbers from FloorSet alone.

Kaplan ♢ \scriptstyle\diamondsuit Ming-Qi Xu ♡ \scriptstyle\heartsuit Wuqian Tang ♡ \scriptstyle\heartsuit Chun-Yao Wang ♡ \scriptstyle\heartsuit Shang-Hong Lai ♡ \scriptstyle\heartsuit Chun-Yi Lee ★ \scriptstyle\bigstar ♡ \scriptstyle\heartsuit National Tsing Hua University ♠ \scriptstyle\spadesuit Kohaku Lab ♣ \scriptstyle\clubsuit Karolinska Institutet △ \scriptstyle\triangle Stockholm University ♢ \scriptstyle\diamondsuit realiz.ai ★ \scriptstyle\bigstar National Taiwan University ∗ \scriptstyle\ast Equal contribution † \scriptstyle\dagger Corresponding author: kohaku@kblueleaf.net Project page: https://kohaku-lab.github.io/Trinity/ Abstract Floorplanning arranges the blocks of a chip and decides their shapes under objectives that press blocks together, short wirelength and a small outline, and constraints that hold them apart, non-overlap, clusters, MIB shapes and boundary blocks. Recent diffusion placers train on reference layouts alone and leave this coupled system to guidance, post-hoc loops and a legalizer, reporting only the endpoint, which hides what the generator contributes. We re-implement four of them under one recipe on FloorSet, score raw, refined and legalized layouts on one scale, and propose Trinity, a flow-matching floorplanner whose six differentiable functions for the constraints and objectives are its training loss term, the energy of a closed-form refiner after sampling and the base of a soft cost for every stage. The network thus learns the correction prior placers apply in their samplers, and sampling needs no guidance. Stage by stage, the training term lowers a plain transformer’s raw soft cost by 26% and matters most at short budgets, the shared refiner decides more of the final cost than the generator and matches a ported placer’s loop in 16 to 660 times fewer steps, Trinity’s refined soft cost is 36% below the best ported pipeline, the soft cost ranks settings as the contest’s hard cost does, and on the FloorSet val set the pipeline reaches a mean hard cost of 1.014 in 1.63 s per case. Figure 1: The network beside each pipeline is the generator that training updates and sampling evaluates. Left: In prior diffusion placers the constraints are absent from training (dashed), differ in form between stages ( ≠ \neq ), and the layouts in between are not measured. Middle: Trinity carries one set of constraint and objective functions, its differentiable physics, through training, refinement, and scoring. Right: Soft cost against refinement budget, each curve starting at the raw sample with zero refinement steps. Faster : the step at which each prior generator under our refiner reaches the soft cost of its own full loop (triangle). Lower : the refined soft cost of the best prior pipeline against ours. 1 Introduction Floorplanning is an early stage of the physical design flow in Electronic Design Automation (EDA). Given a netlist and each block’s target area, floorplanning arranges the position and shape of every block on the chip, and the floorplan bounds what each later stage can achieve. A floorplanner pursues two objectives, short wirelength between connected blocks and a small outline area , and must reach them under hard constraints: a floorplan is feasible only if every block matches its target area, fixed-shape blocks retain their shapes, pre-placed blocks remain in place, and no two blocks overlap. Three soft constraints follow in practice: blocks of a cluster should stay adjacent, multi-instance blocks (MIB) should share one shape, and boundary blocks should touch the die boundary ( ICCAD, 2026 ) . The objectives and constraints pull in opposite directions, and the strongest floorplans sit where the hard constraints bind. Learning-based methods promise to amortize this per-instance optimization into a trained model. Floorplanning moreover suits a generative treatment: an instance admits many strong layouts rather than one optimum, and a generative model drafts complete layouts from this distribution ( Lee et al., 2025 ; Trung and Hy, 2026 ; Yoon et al., 2026 ; Xie et al., 2026 ) . However, such a model learns the distribution of reference layouts rather than the geometry of a single one: a network trained with a squared loss estimates a conditional mean of the reference layouts given its input, and a mean of feasible layouts is not necessarily feasible, since the feasible set is nonconvex. An infeasible draft leaves the constraints to corrections applied after sampling. Such corrections act on a landscape whose couplings belong to floorplanning itself rather than any model: as blocks compete for the same die area, a step that resolves an overlap can scatter a cluster or displace a pre-placed block, and a push toward feasibility may sacrifice the wirelength and outline area that the objectives demand. A generative floorplanner must therefore treat the constraints and objectives as one coupled system, and where this system enters the pipeline determines what the model learns. Existing methods differ in where they place this coupled system, and each choice carries its own cost. Classic floorplanners place it inside the search procedure: simulated annealing ( Wong and Liu, 1986 ) explores topological representations such as the sequence pair ( Murata et al., 1996 ) and the B ∗ -tree ( Chang et al., 2000 ) , in which non-overlap holds by construction, and analytical placement ( Lu et al., 2015 ; Lin et al., 2021 ) minimizes a differentiable relaxation of overlap jointly with wirelength. Since every move faces the constraints and the objectives together, these solvers remain on the boundary, at the price of a search that begins anew on every netlist. Learning-based methods lift this per-instance cost, and the constraints begin to recede from training. Reinforcement learning stays nearest to the classic position, with the constraints written into its actions and the objectives into its reward ( Mirhoseini et al., 2021 ; Lai et al., 2022 ; Lai et al., 2023 ) , although the two do not meet in one function that the policy learns, and the agent is retrained or fine-tuned for every new netlist. Regression abandons the constraints and trains on reference layouts alone ( Liu et al., 2023b ; Amini et al., 2022 ) , which leaves the model exposed to the conditional-mean difficulty above. The recent diffusion placers ( Lee et al., 2025 ; Trung and Hy, 2026 ; Yoon et al., 2026 ; Xie et al., 2026 ) push this coupled system farthest from training: their losses only reproduce the reference layouts, and every correction arrives after the model. The first of these corrections, a hand-tuned guidance term, intervenes during sampling. The finished sample then enters post-hoc optimization loops, and the remaining violations are left to the legalizer. Fig. 1 (left) draws this arrangement. These placers come from macro placement, a task where every shape is fixed: the shape freedom of floorplanning, and its soft constraints, stay outside their scope. The network’s contribution is not measured stage by stage: their papers examine only the endpoint of the pipeline, and each stage expresses the constraints in its own form, which leaves the intermediate layouts without a common measure. At that endpoint, a weak generator behind a strong correction and a strong generator behind a weak one appear identical. The constraints thus migrate from the core of the classic search to the tail of the correction chain. Among the generative placers, the constraints have appeared everywhere except the training loss. Their place in that loss, and its effect on every later stage, nevertheless remain unexplored. Given these observations, the remedy is to move the coupled system into training itself. The constraints can enter the training loss directly, since every objective and constraint of floorplanning measures a geometric quantity of the layout and admits a differentiable expression in the positions and shapes of the blocks. The overlap between two blocks, for instance, shrinks continuously as they separate and reaches zero exactly when the pair satisfies the non-overlap constraint. A weighted sum of these expressions defines an energy, one function that records the constraints and objectives together with the trade-off between them. The energy therefore assigns every layout a graded value rather than a binary indicator of feasibility. Analytical placement already minimizes an energy of this form that couples overlap with wirelength ( Kleinhans et al., 1991 ; Lu et al., 2015 ; Lin et al., 2021 ) . A generative floorplanner can instead place such an energy in its training loss, where each gradient step responds to the reference layouts and the coupled system together. After training, the same expressions determine what a later refinement minimizes and provide a common measure for the layout that each stage produces ( Fig. 1 , middle). On this measure, the intermediate layouts reveal how much the generator and each later stage contribute, a distinction that the endpoint alone conceals. To expose this distinction and place the coupled system in training rather than leave it to corrections after sampling, we propose Trinity , a flow-matching floorplanner whose six differentiable functions for the constraints and objectives are incorporated into its training loss, serve as the energy of its refiner, and form the basis of a soft cost that scores the layout of every stage. Trained with these functions, the network learns the correction that prior placers apply inside their samplers, and sampling runs without guidance ( Section 3 ). Measured stage by stage, the pipeline reveals distinct roles for training and refinement: the training term contributes most when the refinement budget is short, and the refiner accounts for more of the final cost than the generator does. Added to the training of a plain transformer, the six functions alone lower the soft cost of its raw samples by 26% ( Section 4.2 ). With our refiner shared across the generators of four diffusion placers ported to our training recipe, their final costs converge despite a wide spread in raw costs, and on a ported placer’s samples, the refiner reaches the soft cost of that placer’s own loop in 16 to 660 times fewer iterations ( Fig. 1 , right). A comparison of generators therefore calls for a shared refiner. Against the ported pipelines with their own post-hoc loops, the full pipeline of Trinity reaches a refined soft cost 36% below the best of them ( Section 4.3 ). After legalization, Trinity remains ahead of these pipelines under the hard cost of the official contest ( ICCAD, 2026 ) , and on its validation set it reaches a mean hard cost of 1.014 at 1.63 seconds per case on one GPU with parallel legalization ( Section 4.4 ). Contributions. (1) We locate the limit of generative placers in the position of their physics rather than the strength of their networks: the coupled objectives and constraints of floorplanning enter every stage except the training loss. Trinity instead trains on the coupled system directly, with one energy built from six differentiable functions of the layout, and feasibility becomes a property the network learns rather than one that corrections restore. (2) We establish the theory behind this choice: a network trained on reference layouts alone estimates a conditional mean that the nonconvex feasible set does not necessarily contain, whereas the energy term in training approximates constraint guidance inside the sampling loop at no sampling cost. The same analysis selects the clean prediction as the head, the one output an energy can score, and experiment confirms each prediction. (3) We replace the hand-tuned correction loops of prior placers with a refiner that descends the training energy itself, every gradient in closed form. One refiner serves every generator: it carries Trinity and each ported placer below the final cost their own loops reach, and supplies the common ground for comparing generators. (4) We extend the scale of the contest beyond feasibility: our soft cost keeps the objective factor of the hard cost and admits overlap and soft-constraint severity as smooth penalties, and every stage’s layout shares one scale. Since the soft cost agrees with the hard cost on which settings perform better, the sampling and refinement budget can be chosen before the legalizer runs. (5) We lift the fixed-shape assumption that diffusion placers inherited from macro placement: Trinity treats positions and shapes alike and covers the full constraint family of floorplanning, from soft and pre-placed blocks to clusters, boundary blocks, and shared multi-instance shapes, and on the contest’s validation set the full pipeline surpasses the classical annealer at a fraction of its runtime. 2 Related Work Classical optimization and direct learned placement construct layouts through per-instance search, sequential decisions, or joint coordinate prediction: simulated annealing explores sequence pairs and B ∗ -trees ( Wong and Liu, 1986 ; Murata et al., 1996 ; Chang et al., 2000 ; Lin and Chang, 2001 ; Adya and Markov, 2003 ) , analytical placement couples a continuous relaxation of overlap with legalization ( Kleinhans et al., 1991 ; Chen et al., 2008a ; Lu et al., 2015 ; Lin et al., 2021 ) , sequential construction commits one macro per decision under reinforcement learning ( Mirhoseini et al., 2021 ; Cheng and Yan, 2021 ; Lai et al., 2022 ; Lai et al., 2023 ; Geng et al., 2024 ; Geng et al., 2025 ; Gao et al., 2026 ; Shi et al., 2023 ) , and joint prediction regresses every block position from the netlist graph ( Liu et al., 2023b ; Amini et al., 2022 ) . Across the learned lines, block shapes stay fixed at placement time, whereas FloorSet requires the placer to settle a shape for every soft block ( Mallappa et al., 2024 ) . Generative macro placement keeps the fixed-shape setting and learns layout distributions through noise or velocity prediction, with geometric corrections during or after sampling: velocity-based FlowPlace ( Xie et al., 2026 ) applies overlap-free grid projection at each step, while the noise-based MacroDiff+ ( Yoon et al., 2026 ) , ChipDiffusion ( Lee et al., 2025 ) , and DiffPlace ( Trung and Hy, 2026 ) steer sampling with overlap and wirelength gradient guidance before post-hoc loops and legalization. On the objective side, linear transformations between data and noise connect flow matching ( Lipman et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2023a ) , interpolants ( Ma et al., 2024 ) , and noise prediction ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Nichol and Dhariwal, 2021 ; Salimans and Ho, 2022 ) , LACE ( Chen et al., 2024 ) and physics-informed diffusion ( Bastek et al., 2025 ) supervise the clean prediction with constraint losses, and Diffusion Transformers ( Peebles and Xie, 2023 ) supply the backbone, conditioned on the netlist through Graphormer-style attention bias ( Ying et al., 2021 ) , GraphGPS-style message passing ( Rampášek et al., 2022 ) , and Laplacian positional encoding ( Dwivedi and Bresson, 2020 ; Kreuzer et al., 2021 ; Dwivedi et al., 2022 ) . Following JiT ( Li and He, 2026 ) , Trinity predicts the clean layout and trains on the velocity it implies. For variable-shape floorplanning, it combines netlist-conditioned clean prediction in a DiT backbone with constraint supervision through one set of geometric functions for training, refinement, and scoring, and it scores raw, refined, and legalized layouts separately. Section A.4 surveys these lines in full. 3 Methodology 3.1 Problem Formulation The floorplanning problem takes as input n n blocks with target areas a i a_{i} , a weighted netlist A i ​ j A_{ij} and the constraints of Section 1 . Generator. The generator drafts complete layouts from noise, conditioned on the netlist, and carries the physics term in its training loss. A DiT ( Peebles and Xie, 2023 ) with one token per block and the time step as a token ( Bao et al., 2023 ) . The netlist enters as an additive attention bias ( Ying et al., 2021 ) , through the information mover, a gated one-hop graph convolution on the residual stream ( Kipf and Welling, 2017 ; Rampášek et al., 2022 ) , and as two Laplacian eigenvectors in the input coordinates ( Dwivedi and Bresson, 2020 ; Kreuzer et al., 2021 ) (Appendix B.3 ). Following JiT ( Li and He, 2026 ) , the network predicts the clean layout x ^ 0 \hat{x}_{0} and trains on its implied velocity, with t t logit-normal ( Esser et al., 2024 ) , m m the padding mask and the weights λ \lambda , ω k \omega_{k} of Section 4.1 , as follows: ℒ = 𝔼 t , x 0 , x 1 ​ [ ℒ fm + λ ​ U ​ ( x ^ 0 ) ] , ℒ fm = ‖ ( x t − x ^ 0 t − ( x 1 − x 0 ) ) ⊙ m ‖ 2 2 . \mathcal{L}=\mathbb{E}_{t,\,x_{0},\,x_{1}}\bigl[\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{fm}}+\lambda\,U(\hat{x}_{0})\bigr],\qquad\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{fm}}=\bigl\|\bigl(\tfrac{x_{t}-\hat{x}_{0}}{t}-(x_{1}-x_{0})\bigr)\odot m\bigr\|_{2}^{2}. (3) The clean head keeps the physics term inexpensive, since the loss needs a decoded layout and x ^ 0 \hat{x}_{0} is one, whereas a velocity head reaches the same minimizer through a gradient scaled by − t -t and a target that still contains the noise (Proposition D.3 ), which Section 4.2 measures. Sampling follows plain Euler in uniform steps from t = 1 t=1 to 0 0 over NFE \mathrm{NFE} evaluations with no guidance term, and after every step the known answers of the instance enter the sample, a fixed-shape block keeping its ρ i \rho_{i} , a pre-placed block all three coordinates and the blocks of a MIB group the mean of their predicted ρ i \rho_{i} . Refiner. The refiner descends the training energy explicitly once sampling ends, at negligible cost. From each sample at t = 0 t=0 , the refiner takes K K steps of Adam ( Kingma and Ba, 2015 ) on U U under a heavier overlap weight than training, every gradient evaluated in closed form and the same sampling overrides written back after every step. Refinement thus resumes the descent of U U where the proximal step of Proposition 3.1 has vanished at t = 0 t=0 (schedule, sweep and running cost in Appendix E ). Legalizer. The legalizer converts each refined layout into a hard-feasible one while penalizing the displacement it introduces. A sequence-pair relation, under which non-overlap holds by construction, is extracted for every pair of blocks from the refined layout, and one linear program positions the blocks at their decoded shapes under those relations, with the pre-placed blocks pinned, cluster members abutting along a spanning tree of the cluster and coded sides on the outline, and minimizes the chip outline plus the displacement from the refined positions ( Murata et al., 1996 ; Murata and Kuh, 1998 ) . An infeasible program first relaxes the soft rules, flips the conflicting relations and re-solves the program within a bounded number of rounds, and a final contact snap that moves a block only where no overlap appears completes each draw at a hard-feasible final layout (Appendix F ). 4 Experimental Results The experiments evaluate every stage, since endpoint quality alone cannot identify the generator’s contribution. Raw, refined, and legalized layouts therefore share the one scale of Section 3.1 , which tests whether pre-legalization quality persists in feasible layouts and separates generator quality from later optimization. Appendices H to M hold the full tables, Appendix N every data view. 4.1 Experimental Setup Benchmarks/Datasets. We train on MIB-consistent FloorSet-Lite ( Mallappa et al., 2024 ) , whose 996,000 synthetic floorplans span 21 to 120 blocks per instance. Unless stated otherwise, every reported number on our held-out validation set of 12,000 cases averages four draws per case and then across all cases. We evaluate separately on the official FloorSet val set of 100 cases for the official comparison in Table 8 and run one full GSRC evaluation as an external check in Table 8 . Baselines. We re-implement ChipDiffusion ( Lee et al., 2025 ) , DiffPlace ( Trung and Hy, 2026 ) , MacroDiff+ ( Yoon et al., 2026 ) , and FlowPlace ( Xie et al., 2026 ) as comparisons within the learned generative line. Under one training recipe, the ported placers retain their networks, objectives, and post-hoc loops while adopting our latent representation, conditioning, Euler sampler, and overrides, as specified in Section B.4 . The generator comparison excludes sampler-time guidance, which Appendix J evaluates on its own, and grid projection, whereas Section 4.3 includes the post-hoc loops under their released settings. To examine conditional-mean prediction, Reg- z z and Reg- x ​ y ​ w ​ h xywh predict latents and raw boxes on our backbone, with details in Appendix K.2 . The classical comparison uses the FloorSet team’s PARSAC annealer ( Mostafa et al., 2024 ) only on the FloorSet val set, since its published budget of 10 7 10^{7} steps per worker is prohibitive at the 12,000-case scale, with details in Appendix L . Metrics. We evaluate every layout by the quantities in Section 3.1 for cross-stage comparison, with soft cost derived from the shared differentiable physics and hard cost restricted to feasible layouts after legalization. All 66 models share a training recipe of 200,000 steps with batch size 256 and AdamW at an initial learning rate of 2 × 10 − 4 2\times 10^{-4} with cosine decay. This shared recipe uses exponential moving average (EMA) weights and augmentation by rotation, flip, shift, constraint dropout, and wire dropout at ten GPU-hours per model on one RTX 5090, the machine behind every reported timing. The legalizer runs on 16 CPU workers in parallel, and every training ω k \omega_{k} equals one, with further training details in Appendix B.2 . The clean-sample head exposes a layout for direct energy evaluation, which ties its practical role to the theoretical choice of head. The information mover complements this choice through improved constraint objectives. Joint physics training improves every constraint metric without sacrificing the backbone’s wirelength or area.
